title: 35-year-old took on $20K in debt to launch a business from her dining room—now it brings in 8 figures a year
author: Megan Sauer
description: Set Active founder Lindsey Carter shares how she learned to separate her professional stress from her personal life while growing her athleisure company.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Entrepreneurship, Los Angeles, Lifestyle, Lululemon Athletica Inc, Entrepreneurs, Make It, Make It - Success, Make it - Level Up, Make It - Start-ups, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: Set Active CEO Lindsey Carter used to lose sleep, cry to her friends and struggle to be present in her personal life after a rough day at work.

It’s not that she expected entrepreneurship to be easy. Carter took on $20,000 in personal credit card debt and filled her Los Angeles home with inventory when she started the athleisure company in May 2018, she says. Yet years of obstacles — familiar to many an entrepreneur — followed as she tried to break Set Active into a crowded activewear industry. It took her time to figure out how to separate her professional stress from her personal life.

“I started understanding that struggle wasn’t necessarily a sign that something was going wrong. Sometimes it’s just the reality of building something ambitious,” says Carter, 35. “And if I was going to let every setback rob me of my happiness, I’m going to be spending a very long time being unhappy.”

Set Active is no industry giant, but it brought in eight figures in 2025 net sales and is profitable, according to documents reviewed by CNBC Make It. That comes as growth in the broader activewear market has slowed: Women’s activewear spending in the U.S. increased 2% between October 2025 and September 2026, down from 7% over the preceding 12 months, according to data from market research firm Circana.

Activewear still makes up 30% of U.S. apparel spending, says Circana apparel industry analyst Kristen Classi-Zummo. Shoppers these days particularly gravitate toward casual outfits and loungewear, like sweatpants and sweatshirts, over more active items like leggings and sports bras, Classi-Zummo says. That’s good news for Carter, who sells color- and pattern-filled clothing sets that aren’t solely intended for workouts. Set Active’s Instagram posts feature women sitting on pickleball courts or the banks of the Seine in Paris.

Before launching Set Active, Carter ran her own social media company. While shopping around Los Angeles, she struggled to find matching sets of workout clothes she could wear while running errands, meeting a friend for coffee or working from home. “Everything was like yoga poses and upside-down headstands, and I was just like, ‘That’s not me,’” she says.

Her business idea became more real when an associate connected her with a production professional, she says. She decided to order some samples, collected feedback from friends and drew directly on the products with a permanent marker at her dining room table before sending them back to the manufacturer’s designers, she says.

Going into debt to officially launch the business was just the first among many obstacles while growing Set Active. Some were personal: Carter had two children after starting the company and has never taken maternity leave. She now calls that decision “probably one of the biggest mistakes I’ve ever made.”

She experienced what she describes as symptoms of postpartum depression in 2023, and felt like “a horrible version of myself” while simultaneously running the startup. “I let people down. I let friends down. I let employees down and I just wasn’t my best self.”

Other challenges have been professional. In 2026, Set Active has struggled to consistently deliver orders to customers on time, says Carter. The reasons are varied, she says, declining to go into detail, and the stakes are high approaching the holiday shopping season.

On Oct. 19, Carter wrote on Instagram that Set Active would cancel its Black Friday and Cyber Monday product launches until further notice. The company won’t “drop” any clothes until the products arrive in the company’s Los Angeles warehouse, putting a projected $10-plus million in sales during the most popular shopping days of the year at risk, she wrote.

“I’m walking away from a hefty revenue number,” Carter now says, adding: “But at the end of the day, I built this brand on transparency and community, and the customer comes first to me always. And I’d rather make it right with the customer than hit a revenue goal.”

A hard workday can still make her toss and turn at night, but she’s learned how to return home to her family feeling grateful, she says. She gets satisfaction from solving problems and doing a job she believes in, she adds.

“I just take things day by day with the mindset that challenges are opportunities, and I don’t really see them as the enemy,” says Carter. “I think that when you sign up to be an entrepreneur, you’re signing up for what that journey is going to bring.”

title: When someone won't stop talking, try 5 simple ways to get a word in, says expert
author: Dorie Clark
description: Communication expert Dorie Clark shares five steps you can take to help everyone else get a word in "without blowing up the relationship."
keywords: makeit, Articles, Self-improvement, Workplace relationships, Workplace culture, Leadership, Psychology, Lifestyle, Make It, Make It - Psychology and Relationships, Make It - Life, How to Talk to People , source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: We’ve all had a co-worker — or a friend or relative — who takes up way too much airtime. They dominate conversations and make it hard for others to contribute. You might feel there are only two choices: either stay silent and let them control the agenda, or force yourself to interrupt them, which can feel aggressive.

But as a communication strategist who’s consulted for major companies including Google and Microsoft and taught executive education at Columbia Business School and Duke University’s Fuqua School of Business, I know that you can rein them in without blowing up the relationship.
At work, this is obviously easiest if you’re the person’s manager and it’s your responsibility to guide them. But if you’re peers with a good relationship, you can also bring it up directly.

It’s possible the “monopolizer” is self-important and just wants to hear themselves talk. Or maybe they’d welcome your opinion, but they don’t realize that their excessive talking is silencing you and everyone else around them. Either way, their behavior is a problem. It shuts down good ideas, impedes connection and collaboration and often breeds resentment over time.
Here are five ways to deal with someone who never lets anyone else get a word in.
You keep waiting for a pause in this person’s monologue that will allow you to speak, but it never comes.

You’ll need what I call a “break-in line” to interrupt the onslaught and reclaim the conversation. The best ones are short — you need to get them in quickly — and positive, so the other person doesn’t feel corrected or criticized by your interjection.
For example, you can say, “I love this, Brad!” or “Perfect!” or “Yes!” and then rapidly pivot: “I wanted to make a point related to what you just mentioned…”
It may feel rude to interrupt them, but they’re giving you no choice. Your friendly tone buys you enough space — and goodwill — to insert your insight.

Stopping the monopolizer may need to be a team endeavor. Not everyone will know how to speak up in the face of this barrage, so if you have the confidence to do so, you can help make sure others’ voices are heard too.

You can use what I call the “handoff technique” to jump in quickly with the person’s name — which usually catches their attention — pick up on one thing they said and then immediately pass the conversation over to someone else.
For instance, you might say: “Brad, I’m so glad you mentioned that author! Rita, I think you read some of her previous books, right?”

This combination works because you’re stopping them, politely validating that they’ve said something useful and then empowering someone else to speak. It’s hard even for a monopolizer to charge back into the conversation right away, because you’ve specifically asked for someone else’s perspective.

Most bloviators aren’t malicious, in my experience; it’s just become their style. Because they often don’t recognize the broader issue, the two techniques above may get them to stop in the moment, but the problem will recur. If it does, you may eventually want to have a separate conversation with them to name the pattern.

You might say something like: “Brad, I love how you have so many great ideas to share in our team meetings. Your enthusiasm is such an asset! But I’m noticing that other people aren’t always able to share their insights because you’re jumping in so frequently. I know you want to hear their perspectives, too, so I’m bringing this up because it’d be great if you could help make sure everyone has the chance to contribute.”
If the monopolizer is receptive, they may earnestly want others to speak up — and still fall back into their old habits. That’s why it’s a good idea to create an additional safeguard.
You can agree, in advance, on a signal to alert them if they’re talking too much. Maybe it’s a particular phrase, a hand signal or a direct message if you’re on a video meeting.

The exact phrasing and medium matters less than the fact that you’ve created a real-time notification that can help snap them back, so they can start to understand their own patterns and, over time, monitor themselves better so the responsibility doesn’t have to fall on you.

If a monopolizer at work isn’t receptive to your suggestions — or your relationship is distant or fraught enough that you don’t feel comfortable bringing it up — it may be time to escalate the situation and get your manager involved.

Presumably, your boss has seen the issue firsthand. But maybe they didn’t realize how much it was bothering others and holding the team back. You don’t even have to name your coworker directly, though your boss may catch your drift.

You can say: “I’ve noticed that in meetings, sometimes one person dominates the conversation to the point where it seems like others aren’t being heard. I know you want everyone’s best ideas on the table. At the next meeting, can we strategize as a team about the best way to ensure everyone gets airtime?”
Having your boss lead a general “best practices” conversation is a low-pressure way to help improve dynamics without singling anyone out.

Dorie Clark taught executive education for more than a decade at Columbia Business School and Duke University’s Fuqua School of Business. She is a keynote speaker, former presidential campaign spokeswoman, and bestselling author of “The Long Game.” You can subscribe to her e-newsletter here.

title: Open enrollment is a chance to get this ‘sneaky-good’ investment account that can be ‘better than a Roth’
author: Mike Winters
description: During open enrollment, financial planners say HSAs are worth a closer look for their unusual tax advantages and potential as a long-term investment account.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Personal finance, Social issues, Labor economy, Make It, Make It - Money, Make It - Save and Invest, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: With open enrollment season getting underway, health savings accounts are worth considering for more than just paying medical bills.
That’s because you can invest the money in an HSA and let it grow for decades, with tax advantages that can make the account an especially powerful way to save for retirement.

HSAs are “sneaky-good and very underrated” investment tools, says John Bell, a certified financial planner and founder of Free State Financial Planning. For those who are eligible, he generally puts maxing out an employer-sponsored HSA near the top of his saving priorities, just behind getting the full employer match in a 401(k), and ahead of funding a Roth IRA or taxable brokerage account.

That said, you shouldn’t choose a health plan just to get access to an HSA’s investment potential. Whether an HSA-eligible plan makes sense depends first on your healthcare needs and the costs and coverage of the plans available to you, CFPs tell CNBC Make It.
Like the more common flexible spending account, or FSA, an HSA lets you set aside tax-advantaged money for qualified medical expenses, such as doctor visits, prescription drugs and dental care.

One important distinction is that to contribute to an HSA, you generally must be enrolled in a high-deductible health plan. For 2027, such plans have a minimum deductible — the amount you pay out of pocket before coverage kicks in — of $1,750 for individuals and $3,500 for families. FSAs don’t have the same insurance requirement and are often offered alongside more traditional copay insurance plans, which tend to come with higher premiums and lower deductibles.

But HSAs differ from FSAs in a few other important ways. HSAs stay with you if you change jobs, and unlike most FSAs, they don’t come with a “use it or lose it” rule requiring you to spend money in the account over a certain period. Instead, unspent money rolls over from year to year.

And perhaps most importantly — and what makes HSAs “sneaky-good” as an investment tool — the money can often be invested and left to grow for years. That means an HSA can double as a long-term investment account, much like a 401(k) or brokerage account.
Despite that investment potential, relatively few people take advantage of it. Just 11% of HSAs held investments as of midyear 2026, according to Devenir, an HSA research and investment firm.
That’s despite some unusually generous tax advantages for investors.
An HSA combines “the best parts of traditional and Roth IRAs” through what’s commonly called a “triple tax advantage,” says Robert Persichitte, a CFP and CPA at Delagify Financial:

You don’t need an employer to open an HSA, as long as you have an HSA-eligible health plan. And since 2026, people buying their own insurance have more options, as all Bronze and Catastrophic plans sold on the Affordable Care Act marketplace are HSA-eligible. But workplace HSAs can come with additional benefits: An employer may contribute money to the account, and money you put in through your paycheck can often avoid Social Security and Medicare taxes as well.

If you can afford to leave money in your HSA and pay current healthcare expenses out of pocket, CFPs say there can be good reason to hold onto the money for retirement, when healthcare costs tend to rise with age.
A 65-year-old retiring in 2026 can expect to spend an average of $185,500 on healthcare and medical expenses over the course of retirement, according to Fidelity Investments.

“Healthcare is one of the few retirement expenses we can virtually guarantee,” says Corinna Rose, a CFP at Bell Investment Advisors. “Whether it’s prescriptions, Medicare premiums, long-term care costs or routine medical expenses, most retirees will spend money on their health one way or another.”

Another advantage: There’s no time limit on when you can withdraw money from an HSA to cover a past qualified medical expense. For example, if you pay a $5,000 medical bill out of pocket at age 50, you could withdraw $5,000 tax-free at age 65, as long as you kept the necessary records.
Persichitte has used that strategy himself. He waited three years to reimburse himself after breaking his arm, giving the money in his HSA more time to grow.

Taken together, the tax advantages are why Persichitte ranks HSAs so highly. Once you’ve contributed enough to a 401(k) to get the full employer match, he generally recommends maxing out an HSA before putting more money into a 401(k), Roth IRA or taxable brokerage account.
As attractive as HSAs can be as investment accounts, their investment potential alone isn’t a reason to seek one out.

“HSAs are extremely valuable, but don’t make an isolated decision on whether to own one,” says Michael Schramm, a CFA charterholder and author of the forthcoming book “Emotional Finance.” “Instead, step back and ask which health plan’s right for you.”

That means comparing the actual costs and coverage of the plans available to you, including premiums, deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums, along with any money your employer contributes to an HSA, Schramm says.

Higher-deductible plans generally trade lower monthly premiums for higher upfront healthcare costs, Schramm says. That can work well for someone who doesn’t expect to need much medical care. But if you anticipate a lot of medical expenses, you could end up paying thousands of dollars out of pocket before your insurance starts picking up the bill.
Having emergency savings matters, too. An HSA-eligible plan may be easier to manage if you have enough cash set aside to cover your deductible without taking on debt.

That said, there are risks in using the money in your HSA to buy investments. Stocks and bonds have historically rewarded long-term investors, but they can lose value, and past performance doesn’t guarantee future returns. Money you expect to need for near-term medical expenses may be better kept in cash.

For 2027, you can put up to $4,500 into an HSA if you have self-only coverage, or $9,000 if you have family coverage. People age 55 and older can contribute an additional $1,000. Any money your employer contributes counts toward those limits.

And while the money can ultimately be used for purposes other than healthcare, doing so before age 65 generally means paying income tax plus a 20% additional tax. After 65, that additional tax goes away, although nonmedical withdrawals are still generally subject to income tax.

For someone who chooses an HSA-eligible plan and can comfortably handle its potential out-of-pocket costs, however, the HSA can be much more than a way to pay this year’s medical bills. It can be a long-term investment account, too.

title: Avoiding money conversations could be costing you, says Harvard prof.—how to break the ice
author: Ryan Ermey
description: A Harvard Business School professor says difficult money talks can get easier when both sides start with a shared goal.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Personal finance, Lifestyle, Make It, Make It - Money, Make It - Save and Invest, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: My parents and I recently had an awkward conversation.

I’m getting married next year, and it’s shaping up to be quite a shindig. Both sets of parents sent extensive guest lists, and my fiancé and I are doing our best to keep the total headcount under 250.

Things have gotten expensive quickly. And while the bride’s family traditionally bears the bigger financial responsibility for these sorts of things, our wedding is bride-free. So even though my fiancé and I are saving diligently to have the wedding we want, we nevertheless each asked our parents for a contribution.

My parents love the partner I’ve chosen and have been supportive of the engagement. But that didn’t make me any less queasy approaching the conversation. Growing up, money was considered rude to talk about in my household, a setup that’s all too common, says Christina Wing, a professor at Harvard Business School and author of “Unspeakable: The Taboo Topics We Avoid and How to Talk About Them.”
“We were taught at a young age that money is a taboo subject, something that’s impolite to discuss with others,” she writes in her book.

“Money has always had strings attached to it, and so many people use that as a weapon that it’s made us all not want to talk about it,” Wing tells CNBC Make It. “People with a lot of money are fearful they’ll be judged for the decisions they make. People without money don’t want others to know they don’t have it because their self-worth is tied up in it.”
The result, she says, is that people often avoid these conversations altogether. But the consequences of this avoidance are often both emotional and material, she says.

“The cost of silence is that decisions get made without people’s input and without people knowing,” she says, adding that, in the case of money decisions, meaningful sums can be on the line. “Not talking about these things doesn’t make them go away.”
It’s not hard to see how avoiding financial conversations can put you in emotional or financial hot water. Wing cites numerous potential examples:

To avoid these scenarios, Wing says you’ll likely have to have that difficult financial conversation, one that can be made easier by focusing on one key thing: “You have to identify a common goal with the person,” she says.
By identifying a shared objective at the beginning of the conversation, you can help ward off many of the biases and fears that come into play when talking about money, Wing says.

One goal you may have is to make sure your aging parents are comfortable, especially in the case that they become incapacitated or need long-term care. Even if your parents bristle at a potential money talk, you might say, “I don’t need to know what you and mom have. I don’t need to know if I’m getting anything. But I do need to know what my responsibilities would be if something happened to you,” Wing says.

To use a lower-stakes example, imagine a scenario in which you and your friends seemingly have different budgets for outings and group vacations. Waffling on or opting out of these get-togethers because you can’t afford them is likely to cause resentment if the financial aspect goes unaddressed, Wing says. So be upfront about your common goal.
Wing suggests a possible script:

“I love hanging out with you, and I love when you pick restaurants, and we should do those sometimes. But we’d also like to have you over to watch the new Spider-Man movie, and we’re going to cook pizza. Or let’s go for a walk, because my goal is to see you, but I can’t keep spending this much money.”

As it turns out, that’s more or less the tack I took with my parents. I told them what I thought the whole thing would cost and explained that it was important to me that they had all of their people there, that this was a celebration of them and our family as much as it was my marriage. I almost threw up, but they said the number I quoted made sense.

Would it have been easier if we had been talking about money freely as a family since I was a kid? Of course. But it’s better late than never, says Wing — and certainly better than if I had just started planning a wedding assuming that my parents would offer to chip in.

title: Ex-Amex CEO shares when business leaders need to speak up about politics: 'You should care about what happens in our society'
author: Tom Huddleston Jr.
description: Ken Chenault, who served 17 years as American Express CEO, says some political situations call for a firm stance from business leaders.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Leadership, Government and politics, American Express Co, Kenneth Frazier, Merck & Co Inc, Donald Trump, United States, Make It, Make It - Success, Make It - Leadership, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: When a CEO talks politics, people tend to get nervous — especially when the issues don’t seem to directly affect the company.

Yet “some fundamental issues” call for a public stance, even if the subject doesn’t obviously or immediately affect a CEO’s company, former American Express CEO Ken Chenault told CNBC’s “Squawk Box” on Monday. Any threat to democratic institutions or processes in the U.S. can ultimately sow political and economic instability that could have a negative impact on any business, regardless of the sector or industry, he added.

“If you want to build an enduring company, you should care about what happens in our society,” said Chenault, who stepped down as American Express CEO in 2018 after 37 years at the financial services giant, including nearly 17 as chief executive. He currently serves as chairman and managing director of venture capital firm General Catalyst.

CEOs shouldn’t speak out on every political matter, Chenault said. But those seeking lasting success need “long-term perspective” about any risks and opportunities that could ultimately affect their companies, he suggested.

Business leaders often refrain from speaking out on political issues for fear of alienating customers or their own employees. Some companies have found success weaving politics into their public image — outdoor apparel company Patagonia is among the best known — but taking a publicly political stance is most often met with mixed opinions, according to a 2025 study from a group of Ivy League researchers. On the whole, the average person generally prefers CEOs to stay silent on divisive political issues, the study found.

Yet with American voters heading to the polls on Tuesday, Chenault specifically pointed to the issue of voting rights as one that corporate leaders like himself should publicly acknowledge. As the Republican Party braces to potentially lose national and state-level seats in the midterm elections, President Donald Trump has declined to say he would unconditionally accept the electoral results. Instead, the president has promised to accept the results “if they’re honest elections,” The Washington Post reported on Oct. 27.

“If, in fact, the upcoming election is threatened and the verdict of the election is not accepted, that is not an issue that I would be quiet [on],” Chenault said, adding: “Nothing is more fundamental than preserving and strengthening our democracy [and] the fundamental right to vote.”

Political instability can hurt a country’s economy, research suggests. One potential path for democratic erosion to harm business: A breakdown of the rule of law can scare off investors looking to deploy capital or build new companies, Princeton University political scientist Layna Mosley found in a July 2023 report published by nonpartisan organizations The Brookings Institution and States United Democracy Center.

As American Express CEO, Chenault weighed in publicly on some political issues that did have an immediate impact on his company. One of his more prominent stances was an acknowledgment of the financial industry’s need to adapt and accept additional regulatory oversight following the 2008 financial crisis, for example.

More recently, Chenault has spoken somewhat frequently about the importance of robust voting rights. In March 2021, he and former Merck CEO Ken Frazier called on corporate leaders to push back on political efforts to restrict voting access in the U.S. In particular, Chenault — one of the first few Black CEOs of a Fortune 500 company, upon his appointment at American Express in 2001 — spoke out against policies that voting rights groups have criticized as disproportionately disenfranchising voters of color.

“Corporations have to stand up. There is no middle ground,” Chenault told “Squawk Box” on March 31, 2021. “This is about all Americans having the right to vote, but we need to recognize the special history of the denial of the right to vote for Black Americans, and we will not be silent.”

title: Ghosted after a job interview? There's a website for that—and thousands of frustrated job seekers have weighed in
author: Sophie Caldwell
description: Being ghosted during the hiring process can be frustrating and demoralizing for candidates. Gary Meyer created a space for them to vent.
keywords: makeit, Articles, United States, Labor economy, Toronto, Personnel, Apple Inc, Salesforce Inc, JPMorgan Chase & Co, Make It, Make It - Work, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: Gary Meyer didn’t intend to become a ghostbuster. But his website, Did They Ghost You, has become an outlet for thousands of frustrated job seekers who have been ghosted by employers.

Based on anonymous reports — 2,888 at last count — the site tracks and ranks the companies that are most often accused of abruptly ceasing contact with candidates, including some of the biggest names in the S&P 500.

Ghosting is a widespread issue. A recent report from hiring platform Greenhouse found that 45% of job seekers who made it to the interview stage of a hiring process said they were ghosted by an employer afterward, based on a survey of 1,200 U.S. candidates conducted in September 2026.

Meyer, 42, an artificial intelligence-focused marketing consultant who lives in Toronto, created Did They Ghost You in June after listening to his friends vent about interviewing with companies and then never hearing back.

He never intended for the website to be more than a “fun little side project,” but when he shared a link to his site on LinkedIn, the reports started pouring in. He says that within the first few days, the site received more than two million visitors: “Clearly, it struck a bit of a nerve.”

Meyer, who reads and approves each report himself, says he fielded five or six new submissions every minute at the height of the site’s popularity over the summer. To protect people’s identities, Meyer typically doesn’t publish the contents of the report, and his site doesn’t track personal information. Each report contributes to an overall tally of ghosting incidents.
“Was told that I was the preferred candidate by the Director of HR in a debrief immediately following the final interview and then just didn’t hear back,” one report featured on the site said.
“Ghosted, then reposted their ad a week later,” said another.
Meyer’s definition of being ghosted by an employer doesn’t include applying for a job and never hearing back — unfortunately, “that’s part and parcel” of the job market today, he says.
His website is for people who make it through several steps of the hiring process and then never hear from the company again.

“These are people who have gone through multiple rounds of interviews, met with people, flown to various states or cities for the interview and then right at the end, just nothing, no response, nothing,” he says.
Part of the reason he created the site is to let those job seekers know they’re not alone, he says.

“I think a huge part of what makes it hurt so much when you get ghosted is the assumption is that you’ve screwed up so badly that you’re not worth responding to, that you’re not even worth an email,” he says.

It’s easy for job seekers to blame themselves when they get ghosted, according to career coach Phoebe Gavin, but it’s really a failure on the company’s part to practice “basic etiquette” in the hiring process.

“The hiring process requires a great deal of unpaid labor from candidates, and it is a reasonable expectation that you will receive some sort of communication, that you will be treated with some sort of dignity,” she says.
Although it doesn’t excuse their actions, there are a few common reasons that a company might ghost a candidate, Gavin says.

Especially at small companies, managers are often tasked with supervising the hiring process on top of their regular duties. While juggling all those responsibilities, it’s easy for a candidate to get “lost in the shuffle,” she says.

Another possibility is that there could be some behind-the-scenes factors that the hiring manager can’t share with an external candidate, like a budget cut, hiring freeze or leadership turnover, Gavin says.
Still, “candidates deserve to hear from hiring managers regardless,” she says.

Meyer says he doesn’t intend to turn Did They Ghost You into the next Glassdoor. The site’s popularity “got a little bit overwhelming,” he says, and he currently has a backlog of reports to read and approve.
He plans to keep running the website, but “the best case scenario is that this problem gets fixed, and there’s no point in having the site anymore.”

title: A 5-word phrase you use all year could tank your performance review, says expert—what to say instead
author: Melody Wilding
description: It can "tank your performance review,” says executive coach Melody Wilding. She shares four ways to show your individual impact while giving others credit.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Careers, Career advice, Career coaching, Leadership, Make It, Make It - Get Ahead, Make It - Life, How to Talk to People , source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: There’s a common five-word phrase that sounds humble and collaborative, but can also undermine your hard-earned impact and even tank your performance review: “It was a team effort.”

Of course, you should give recognition to your colleagues where it’s due. The problem is when you downplay your role so much that your individual contribution disappears. If everything was a team effort, then what skills did you bring to the table? What outcomes did you create? It’s much harder for your boss to justify a raise or promotion with no concrete data about your personal performance.

As an executive coach, I’ve spent the past 15 years helping high performers at organizations like Google, Amazon and JPMorgan build influence with powerful people. I’ve observed that those who emerge from performance review season with the biggest opportunities proactively communicate the value of their work. They don’t simply hope their boss can decipher and remember what they accomplished.

You can still be fair and generous toward others. But instead of insisting that “it was a team effort” and leaving it at that, follow up with these strategies to advocate for yourself in your performance review conversations and year-round.
Even if a project was a collaboration, someone still had to choose what to prioritize, how to tackle the plan and how to respond when things changed.

Clarify your role in the choices that drove the group’s execution or identify what obstacles you personally cleared. This puts on prominent display your judgment and problem-solving, which are two essential skills for higher-level responsibilities.
Compare what you did on a recent project to what you handled six or 12 months before. Measuring yourself against your own past performance makes it easier for your boss to grasp your growth.
For instance, explain how your scope or level of influence has grown. Perhaps you’re managing larger accounts, presenting work directly to executives or setting project strategy.
Reference something concrete you created that has added value to the team effort. Maybe you built a dashboard, documented a process or designed a template.
This proves your efforts have a longer-lasting impact on how the team operates. Explain how this asset has now made everyone’s work faster, more productive or more consistent going forward.

I’ve seen how people tend to take someone seriously when they come recommended. So mention how a colleague specifically sought you out for an opinion, an executive tapped you for an initiative or someone praised your effort. It’s evidence that your individual contribution stood out within a larger project.

Your performance review is one of the most important career moments of the year. Take the opportunities you have leading up to it — and all year long — to make your results visible to your boss and to build the case for better projects and more money.

Melody Wilding, LMSW is an executive coach, human behavior professor and author of ”Managing Up: How to Get What You Need from the People in Charge.” Get her free training, 5 Steps to Speak Like a Senior Leader, here.

paragraphs: This Cookie Notice (“Notice”) explains how Versant Media LLC and its affiliates (“Versant,” “our,” “us,” or “we”), along with our partners, including advertisers and vendors, use cookies and similar tracking technologies on our websites, applications, and other online services (the “Services”). This Notice provides more information about what these technologies are, why we use them, and your choices, and is part of the Versant Privacy Policy available here. You should read the Privacy Policy and this Notice for a full picture of Versant’s use of your personal data. Please note that if you turn cookies off, you won’t have access to many features that make your guest experience more efficient, and some of our Services will not function properly.

Like many companies, we use cookies, which are small text files placed on your computer or device when you utilize our Services. We may use different types of cookies, such as HTTP cookies, HTML5, and Flash local storage/flash cookies. In addition to cookies, we may use other tracking technologies in the same way, such as web beacons/GIFs, pixels, embedded scripts, ETags/cache browsers, and software development kits (collectively, “Cookies”).

Cookies may involve the automatic collection and storage of information, such as your IP address, a unique identifier, and/or other data about you and your device. Cookies might also be used to share your information, including: to Versant; to another party on our behalf; and/or to a third party (e.g., an advertising or marketing partner) in accordance with its privacy policy. Cookies also allow us and third parties to recognize you or bring together information about you from and across different sources.
As explained more fully below, Versant, our partners, and other third parties use Cookies for different purposes on our Services:

Strictly Necessary: These Cookies are required for Service functionality, including for system administration, delivering requested content and features, security and fraud prevention, to identify and fix technical issues, authenticate your identity, and to enable purchasing capabilities. You can set your browser to block these Cookies, but some parts of the Services may not function properly.

Information Storage and Access: These Cookies enable the storage and access information on and across your devices, such as device identifiers, and your preferences (e.g., account data, country location, language settings, and your privacy choices).

Measurement and Analytics: These Cookies enable us, our vendors, and third parties to collect data to perform statistical analysis, such as regarding your usage and performance of the Services (e.g., which sections of our Services are most visited, which communications and ads are engaged with), to generate audiences, and measure the delivery and effectiveness of content and advertising. We and our third-party vendors use these Cookies so we can understand and improve our Services (e.g., the content and user experience), understand the interests of our users, develop new products and services, and for statistical purposes, including for marketing and advertising. They are also used to recognize you and provide further insights across platforms and devices for the above purposes.

Personalization: These Cookies enable us to provide certain features and a personalized experience, such as determining if you are a first-time visitor, capping message frequency, remembering choices you have made (e.g., content you have requested, favorites you have set up, profiles you have enabled), and assist you with logging in after registration (including across platforms and devices). These Cookies also allow your device to receive and send information, so you can see and interact with ads and content.
Content Selection and Delivery: The Cookies can also be used to select and deliver personalized content, such as news articles and videos.

Ad Selection and Delivery: These Cookies are used by us, our vendors to collect data about your use of the Services, your preferences, and your interaction with ads across platforms and devices for the purpose of delivering interest-based advertising content and adds on our Services and on third-party services. title: I've studied hundreds of high-achieving kids. The No. 1 secret to their success—and parents should teach it early
author: Jennifer Breheny Wallace
description: Parenting expert Jennifer Breheny Wallace has spent six years studying hundreds of high-achieving kids. Here's why she says a "mattering mindset" is the secret to their success, and how parents can cultivate it from a young age.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Mental health, Relationships, Lifestyle, Parenting, Education, Make It Contributors, New York City, Make It, Make It - Success, Make It - Life, Make It - Raising Successful Kids, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: As students head back to school this fall, many parents feel the urge to do more — to book the tutor, add the extra math lesson, or squeeze in one more after-school activity “just in case.”
The impulse comes from love and wanting our kids to have opportunities. But somewhere along the way, opportunity can turn into pressure.

During my six years of researching hundreds of high-achieving kids, I’ve found that the real engine behind long-term success is believing that your worth comes from your inherent value and your ability to make a positive impact on the world.
I call it a “mattering mindset.”
DON’T MISS: How to Build a Standout Personal Brand: Online, In Person, and At Work
Many young people today are motivated by the fear that if they fall short, they will be less loved or accepted, as if their value hinges on their performance.

In 2021, I partnered with a Baylor University researcher to investigate the impact of achievement culture among young adults. Our survey — which was published in my book “Never Enough” — of nearly 500 students revealed a sobering finding: More than half believed their parents’ love fluctuated based on their performance.
Psychologists call this “conditional regard,” or parental affection that depends on a child meeting certain expectations, whether academic, athletic, or behavioral.

Children raised on conditional regard can become so afraid of mistakes that even minor setbacks can rattle their sense of self. It can erode self-worth, accelerate burnout, and leave them feeling purposeless once the accolades stop coming or vulnerable to depression when they experience setbacks.

We have to help our kids build a mattering mindset from the start. When children know they are valued despite the outcome, they are freed to take healthy risks, to learn from mistakes, to push harder, and to recover faster.

Become an expert in who they are. What makes them light up? What challenges do they hide? What strengths might others overlook? The more we understand their quirks and talents, the more they feel seen for their unique selves. Feeling known and loved is powerful fuel.
When your child fails — gets cut from the team, bombs a test — remind them their value isn’t up for debate.

One mother I interviewed uses this exercise: She holds up a $20 bill. “What’s it worth?” she asks. Then she crumples it and dunks it in water. “What’s it worth now?” Still $20. No matter the setbacks, its value hasn’t changed, and neither has theirs.
All children want to do well. If they aren’t thriving, take a step back and ask why. Is it an undiagnosed learning difference? A social conflict? A teaching style mismatch? Struggles are clues.
When we express anger over a child’s performance, it can break the parent-child connection. Curiosity preserves your relationship, and is a gateway to clean fuel.

Let them know when their actions make a difference. Whether it’s comforting a sibling, brightening a friend’s day, or coming up with a clever solution, take the time to remind them that their value goes far beyond their achievements.

Too often, we’re so focused on preparing kids for the future that we forget to show them the joy we feel simply by being their parent. At least once a day, show warmth and affection regardless of performance. Let them know they are just as cherished on a bad day as on a good one.

If I could offer one piece of advice to parents this fall, it would be to worry less about the grades and more about the mindset you’re helping cultivate in your child — the one that fuels lifelong achievement.

Jennifer Breheny Wallace is an award-winning journalist and author of the New York Times bestseller ”Never Enough: When Achievement Culture Becomes Toxic — and What We Can Do About It.” She lives in New York City with her husband and three teens. You can follow her on Instagram @jenniferbrehenywallace.

title: I'm a psychologist who studies couples: People in the happiest relationships do 1 thing differently after time apart—whether it's hours, days or weeks
author: Mark Travers
description: Psychologist Mark Travers argues that the first few minutes after time apart are key to a close, happy relationship, and shares five tips to get them right.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Mark Travers, Relationships, Marriage, Self-improvement, Psychology, Mental health, Lifestyle, Personal finance, Make It, Make It - Life, Make It - Psychology and Relationships, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: There’s a two-minute window every evening when couples can either strengthen their bond with each other or unknowingly weaken it.

In my experience as a psychologist who studies couples, what separates the happy couples from the unhappy ones isn’t necessarily how often they argue or how much time they have together. It’s whether the two people are genuinely in contact with each other’s lives.

Partners in happy relationships know what the other one is really going through, week after week. The unhappy ones have often slipped into a kind of parallel coexistence, where they share a home and a calendar and not much else.
That difference can be built or lost in moments that may feel too small to matter. I call them “reentry moments.”

“Reentry moments” are the first minute or two when a couple comes back together after time apart. These reunions follow any period of temporary physical separation, whether that’s a workday, a weekend away with friends or a four-day work trip.
They serve three key functions:
Let’s say your wife mentioned in the morning that she had a presentation that day. You get home and see her, as usual, with her laptop on the couch. You ask her, “How was your presentation?”

She stops typing, sets the laptop on the coffee table and tells you that no one really responded to it, and just thanked her and moved on. She spent the rest of her afternoon turning the presentation over in her head, trying to figure out what went wrong.

Connecting as soon as you reunite keeps you from misreading each other. If your wife is still thinking about the presentation and you ask whether she booked the rental car for your trip next week, the annoyance in her response can sound like annoyance with you. You might snap back, and now you’re arguing about the rental car when neither of you cares about it.

There’s a longer-term benefit, too. When your partner knows the first few minutes at home will be met with interest rather than judgment or indifference, they don’t have to decide what’s worth telling you and what to keep to themselves. They can just walk in knowing they’re entering their safe landing space.

Early in a relationship, nobody has to work hard to harness this moment. You simply want the details of your partner’s day, and if you get the three-word version, you ask again. Years in, you may stop following up.

You might slip into a routine where you share a greeting, ask a question about dinner or tomorrow’s schedule and go about your evening. Nothing overtly unkind happens in that exchange, and both partners might describe it as “fine.” But you know slightly less about your partner with each flubbed reentry.

After a few hundred repetitions, you start working from an out-of-date picture of your partner. You don’t know their new manager has suddenly started checking in on them three times a day. Or that they got into it with their sister on the phone an hour ago. So when they’re unusually quiet at dinner, you might assume that something is wrong between the two of you.

Skipping this small but crucial moment makes it harder to understand and anticipate your partner’s needs, whether that means taking over a chore, canceling a plan or leaving them alone for an hour. Being well-meaning but uninformed might look the same to your partner as not caring.
Eventually, you can lose more than just information; you start losing the close connection you share with your partner.
Getting it right means deliberately stepping out of the “How was your day?” routine and trying something different:
Over time, taking these steps can be part of what keeps two people attuned and responsive to each other rather than simply living side by side.

Mark Travers, Ph.D., is a psychologist who specializes in relationships. He holds degrees from Cornell University and the University of Colorado Boulder. He is the lead psychologist at Awake Therapy, a telehealth company that provides online psychotherapy, counseling and coaching. He is also the curator of the popular mental health and wellness website Therapytips.org.

title: I retired in the No. 1 country Americans want to move to most—I don't regret it: 'We save about $5,000 per month'
author: Alex Trias
description: When he was 41, Alex Trias walked away from a high-paying law career. Now he lives in Portugal, the No. 1 country Americans want to move to the most. The early retiree shares the most life-changing lessons he's learned so far.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Retirement planning, Washington D.C., Portugal, Make It Contributors, Make It, Make It - Life, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: In 2011, I walked away from a six-figure law career and retired at age 41. I thought I was prepared financially. But emotionally? Not so much.

After decades of working, I was used to the sense of purpose that came with a career, and I assumed I’d have to give that up once I stopped working. My biggest fear took the form of one major uncertainty: What would I do with all that unstructured time?

Fast forward 14 years later, and my days are anything but idle. My wife and I now live in Portugal, the No. 1 country Americans want to move to. I spend my free time enjoying local food with friends and hiking the wildflower-dotted coastal trails. Retiring early is one of the best decisions I’ve ever made ... but I remember how overwhelming it felt at the start.
Here’s what I’ve learned so far in early retirement, and why I don’t regret it.

I followed a predictable path for most of my adult life: law school, summer associate gigs, and eventually a stable legal career. Then came the 2008 financial crisis. The firm I worked for collapsed — and with it, my sense of direction. I couldn’t picture myself doing anything other than practicing law.

I could’ve stayed in the industry. But instead, I chose the unknown. Most people think early retirement is about not working anymore. But it’s about redefining your identity without a roadmap. That required a mindset shift: I had to become an explorer.

That mindset brought us to Portugal, a country where we didn’t speak the language, didn’t know anyone, and had no idea what to expect day-to-day. It was disorienting at first. But the uncertainty became our motivation to grow, learn, and build a fulfilling life from scratch.
If you’re delaying retirement because you don’t know what comes next, that might be exactly why it’s worth doing. Uncertainty could be your opportunity to travel down paths you’ve never imagined.
When we first retired, my wife and I assumed we’d gradually draw down our savings over time and hope it would last. But something surprising happened: Our net worth kept growing.
A major reason is that living in Portugal drastically reduced our expenses. Here’s what we save annually compared to our old life in Washington, D.C.:
In total, we estimate that we save about $5,000 per month just by living abroad.

We follow the same financial strategy we did while working: We live below our means, reinvest the difference, and let compounding do the work. The only difference is that now, instead of salaries, our income comes from investments.
Retirement doesn’t have to be the end of building wealth. It can even be the beginning of a more sustainable, intentional version of it.
Whether you’re working or not, most of us want the same thing: to feel like we matter and are making a contribution.
When we first retired, we had a built-in sense of purpose as parents to a young child. We joined school activities, studied the local language, and built a new life in Lisbon.
But when our daughter went off to college, we were back to square one. Our schedules emptied out, and we faced the same question we did in 2011: What do we do with all this time?
Before diving into hobbies or commitments, we made a plan. We identified six core priorities that bring meaning to our lives:
Once we had those priorities in place, it became easier to build a routine that felt fulfilling.

Today, my wife volunteers at our tennis club, takes pottery and Dutch lessons, and plays sports. I’m focused on writing, freelance retirement coaching, and helping a local nonprofit as a consultant. We host dinner parties, explore new recipes, and take short trips around Europe.
With the right mindset, early retirement can be the perfect new starting point. You just have to be willing to embrace it.
Alex Trias is a retired attorney. He and his wife have been living in Portugal since 2015. He writes about tax planning, investing, early retirement and expat life on Substack.

In 2011, I walked away from a six-figure law career and retired at age 41. I thought I was prepared financially. But emotionally? Not so much.
	After decades of working, I was used to the sense of purpose that came with a career, and I assumed I’d have to give that up once I stopped working. My biggest fear took the form of one major uncertainty: What would I do with all that unstructured time?
	Fast forward 14 years later, and my days are anything but idle. My wife and I now live in Portugal, the No. 1 country Americans want to move to. I spend my free time enjoying local food with friends and hiking the wildflower-dotted coastal trails. Retiring early is one of the best decisions I’ve ever made ... but I remember how overwhelming it felt at the start.
	Here’s what I’ve learned so far in early retirement, and why I don’t regret it.
	I followed a predictable path for most of my adult life: law school, summer associate gigs, and eventually a stable legal career. Then came the 2008 financial crisis. The firm I worked for collapsed — and with it, my sense of direction. I couldn’t picture myself doing anything other than practicing law.
	I could’ve stayed in the industry. But instead, I chose the unknown. Most people think early retirement is about not working anymore. But it’s about redefining your identity without a roadmap. That required a mindset shift: I had to become an explorer.
	That mindset brought us to Portugal, a country where we didn’t speak the language, didn’t know anyone, and had no idea what to expect day-to-day. It was disorienting at first. But the uncertainty became our motivation to grow, learn, and build a fulfilling life from scratch.
	If you’re delaying retirement because you don’t know what comes next, that might be exactly why it’s worth doing. Uncertainty could be your opportunity to travel down paths you’ve never imagined.
	When we first retired, my wife and I assumed we’d gradually draw down our savings over time and hope it would last. But something surprising happened: Our net worth kept growing.
	A major reason is that living in Portugal drastically reduced our expenses. Here’s what we save annually compared to our old life in Washington, D.C.:
	In total, we estimate that we save about $5,000 per month just by living abroad.
	We follow the same financial strategy we did while working: We live below our means, reinvest the difference, and let compounding do the work. The only difference is that now, instead of salaries, our income comes from investments.
	Retirement doesn’t have to be the end of building wealth. It can even be the beginning of a more sustainable, intentional version of it.
	Whether you’re working or not, most of us want the same thing: to feel like we matter and are making a contribution.
	When we first retired, we had a built-in sense of purpose as parents to a young child. We joined school activities, studied the local language, and built a new life in Lisbon.
	But when our daughter went off to college, we were back to square one. Our schedules emptied out, and we faced the same question we did in 2011: What do we do with all this time?
	Before diving into hobbies or commitments, we made a plan. We identified six core priorities that bring meaning to our lives:
	Once we had those priorities in place, it became easier to build a routine that felt fulfilling.
	Today, my wife volunteers at our tennis club, takes pottery and Dutch lessons, and plays sports. I’m focused on writing, freelance retirement coaching, and helping a local nonprofit as a consultant. We host dinner parties, explore new recipes, and take short trips around Europe.
	With the right mindset, early retirement can be the perfect new starting point. You just have to be willing to embrace it.

title: Binance loses $6.3 billion in crypto heist—what happens to your money when an exchange gets hacked
author: Mike Winters
description: Crypto exchanges make it easier to buy, sell and store digital assets, but they come with risks, too.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Computer crime, Fraud and false statements, United States, Make It, Make It - Money, Make It - Save and Invest, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: A record-breaking hack at Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, is a reminder of the risks investors take when trusting a company to hold their digital tokens.

Binance said Friday that the security breach affected about $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto hack on record. Around $3 billion of the affected assets has been frozen on blockchain networks, and the exchange says it has begun recovering some of them.

Binance’s initial investigation suggests hackers gained access to the firm’s withdrawal systems and were able to make unauthorized transfers from the exchange’s crypto wallets, according to the company. The company says it has found no evidence that the private keys controlling those wallets were leaked and is still investigating the full scope of the breach.

The company says it will cover customers’ losses. Binance maintains a roughly $1 billion emergency fund known as SAFU, which was created to protect customers in the event of a security breach. The company initially said SAFU and company funds would cover the losses, and has since said it has set aside more than $6.3 billion of its own funds.

For crypto investors, the Binance breach highlights one of the risks of keeping assets on an exchange. While exchanges make it easier to buy, sell and store crypto, what happens after a hack can vary widely, including whether customers get their money back.

Crypto exchange hacks aren’t uncommon. Hackers stole roughly $1.5 billion from Dubai-based exchange Bybit in 2025, while Seychelles-registered Bitget lost more than $387 million in a hack in September 2026.

But a hack doesn’t necessarily mean customers will lose their money permanently. Stolen assets can sometimes be recovered or frozen — preventing the hackers from moving or cashing them out — and exchanges may also have insurance, dedicated emergency funds or other company resources available to cover losses.

In Binance’s case, roughly half of the affected assets have already been frozen, preventing some of the stolen crypto from being moved. Its roughly $1 billion SAFU emergency reserve provides another backstop, if needed.

Customers don’t always recover stolen digital assets quickly. New Zealand exchange Cryptopia was forced into liquidation months after a 2019 hack in which about NZ$30 million in crypto was stolen. The liquidation process stretched on for years, with the first distributions finally beginning in 2024.

“When you leave crypto on an exchange, you are relying on that company’s controls and its balance sheet,” says Martin Mulyadi, YHB Endowed Chair in Accounting and professor of accounting at Shenandoah University. “A pledge to make customers whole is only as strong as the resources behind it.”

When considering where to transact in and hold crypto, start by researching the exchange itself. The Securities and Exchange Commission recommends searching for customer complaints and checking how the exchange is regulated.

U.S. customers can also check whether an exchange is registered with the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, using its online database. Registration can help confirm that you’re dealing with an identifiable business operating within the U.S. regulatory system, though FinCEN cautions that registration isn’t an endorsement of the company.

Crypto experts also recommend reading an exchange’s user agreement or terms of service. Some exchanges might have separate custody agreements or risk disclosures that are worth checking, too, Mulyadi says.

Look for language explaining who owns your crypto and what the exchange can do with it. Phrases such as “you retain title” or assets being “held for your benefit” are good signs, Mulyadi says. Check whether customer assets are kept separate from the exchange’s own, which can offer extra protection if the company fails. And find out whether the exchange can lend or otherwise use your crypto, which can expose your assets to additional risk.
In the user agreement, check the exchange’s limitation-of-liability section, Mulyadi says, and look at what insurance coverage the exchange offers and what it actually covers.
“If a refund after a hack is at the exchange’s discretion, it’s a goodwill gesture, not a promise,” Mulyadi says.

Even strong language in the terms isn’t a guarantee that your assets will be safe. FTX, the popular crypto exchange that collapsed in 2022, misappropriated billions of dollars in customer funds even though its terms said those assets belonged to customers, Mulyadi says.
If you don’t want to hold your crypto through an exchange, there’s another option known as “self-custody.”

With self-custody, you use your own crypto wallet and control the private keys used to authorize transactions on the blockchain. Wallets typically come with a recovery phrase — essentially a master password that can be used to restore access to the wallet if you lose it.
That gives you control of your crypto without relying on an exchange, but it also makes you responsible for keeping that information safe.
And for anyone who’s ever lost or forgotten a password, the risks of self-custody are real. With self-custody, there is “no help desk if you lose your recovery phrase,” Mulyadi says.

For many investors, Mulyadi says a middle ground is keeping only what they actively trade on an exchange and holding longer-term assets themselves, as long as they understand how to safely store and recover them.
“Coins on an exchange are a promise from a company; coins in your own wallet are a responsibility you can’t hand off,” Mulyadi says.

title: I spent more than $1,100 to run the New York City Marathon—here’s what was worth the money
author: Kamaron McNair
description: I spent $1,161 to train for and run the 2026 New York City Marathon. Here's what I bought, what failed and what felt worth the money.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Lifestyle, Nike Inc, Amazon.com Inc, Gap Inc, eBay Inc, Make It, Make It - Money, Make It - Spend, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: I won the lottery in March. Unfortunately, not the Powerball jackpot, but a decent consolation: a chance to run the TCS New York City Marathon on Sunday.

The race lottery came with slightly better odds than the recent billion-dollar lotto draws, but it still surprised me to be among 1% of the 240,000 applicants who secured a bib, according to New York Road Runners, the organization behind the world-renowned event.

As soon as I got my acceptance email in March 2026, my credit card got hit with the $333 entry fee. I knew that would happen when I signed up, but I did not expect to actually be paying that fee, or to have to start training to run 26.2 miles through all five boroughs.

In the months leading up to the race, I hoped to avoid a spending marathon. I was in the process of paying down five figures of credit card debt, and knew I didn’t want to rack that back up buying every cute running outfit or purportedly “necessary” accessory advertised on my social media feed.

Running has historically been understood as an affordable sport. The only equipment you absolutely need is clothing and a pair of shoes, and the latter is technically optional. But as the sport has exploded in popularity, so have the products and brands catering to runners. Even a casual runner may find it difficult to find a good pair of running shoes under $100, and the price tag only goes up with shoes and gear purported to help you run your best.

“It’s become easier to spend a lot of money on running. There are more things you can buy, and it can start to feel like every item is something you need,” says Steve Mura, a coach with New York Road Runners. Items like watches, shoes, specialized water bottles and recovery tools “might serve a purpose, but the total can add up quickly,” he says.

I knew I would need some new equipment to prepare for the marathon, but I committed myself to trying to only buy what I felt I really needed. In the end I still spent $1,161 including my race fee. Here’s what I bought and what I felt was really worth the money.

I’ve been casually running since 2020, so I didn’t go into training without any gear. I had a few pairs of running shorts, plenty of T-shirts and a good pair of Brooks trainers. But as I started upping my mileage, I needed some upgrades. Between April and the end of June, I spent $171 on new clothes from Old Navy, a fresh pair of Brooks, a tub of Squirrel’s Nut Butter to prevent chafing and a monthly subscription for a training app, Runna.

The Old Navy haul proved to be a bit of a bust. The shorts and bra I got were good for a few runs, but made me chafe as the temperatures and my distances increased. I’d worn out my previous running shoes soon after I started training, so I invested in a new pair and was happy to get them on sale for about $80 less than what they usually cost. I used the Runna app as my training guide because I didn’t really know where to begin with my plan.

In July and August, I ran a total of just over 216 miles and spent about $327. That includes two months of Runna subscription charges and two more trips to Old Navy — but for better pieces this time. Additionally, I bit the bullet and got some premium gear from Bandit, an independent running apparel brand that started in Brooklyn in 2020.

I really tried to resist the company’s $88 shorts and matching $78 top. But I learned over many runs that I have two requirements for good running shorts: that they have pockets and don’t ride up. Bandit’s offering definitely met the pockets requirement and reviews told me they would not move, a fact I can now confirm. The top was less of a necessity, but it is now the best sports bra I own and thus far has not caused me any chafing. I also got socks from running sock brand Feetures. They were more affordable than other premium sock offerings, and I got four pairs for around $57.

I err on the side of affordability when it comes to clothes shopping, especially for stuff I work out in. However, training for a marathon quickly taught me the difference between good enough gear and performance wear. I love my Old Navy pieces for lighter workouts, but the cotton material isn’t great for longer runs.

I started experimenting with fuel options as my long runs started exceeding 15 miles in August. First I stuck to snacks I had in my home already, like dried mango or gummy bears. Then I bought a 12-pack of Honey Stinger gels for $20. That felt expensive for what amounts to sugar and salt. But they’re easy to carry and do their job of efficiently delivering carbs and electrolytes during a long workout.

I almost got through September with my Runna subscription as my only expense, but I hit the limit on my running shoes. After a particularly painful long run, I realized I’d racked up over 375 miles on the shoes I bought in May, and I felt it. While running shoes generally can have a lifespan between 300 to 500 miles, some experts encourage runners to rotate a couple of pairs of shoes to get the most out of them. I was wearing these for just about every run.

Initially, I tried to replace them with a gently used pair I got on eBay for $59. When they arrived, however, the insoles had been replaced and the soles had a little more wear than I was comfortable with. I returned them and bought a brand new pair. Unfortunately, I couldn’t get a pair on sale this time, so I wound up paying $195 on Amazon.

In October, with less than a month until the marathon, I completed a 21-mile run that made me confident I was ready for the race. I spent about $47 on a few final items that I could probably live without but will hopefully help the day go smoothly. Instead of more gels, I got a pack of honey packets to use as fuel for a better price of about $9 for 20.

For race day, I got an $11 pair of running sleeves and a 2-pack of portable phone chargers for $15. I’ve seen many TikTok videos about what you “need” at the starting village — runners typically arrive a couple of hours before their actual start time, so veterans generally encourage you to bring some essentials to stay warm and keep yourself and your phone fueled.

Finally, I splurged on a Nike marathon sweatshirt to commemorate the experience, not to run in. It was $65, which felt like a steal when some basic Nike sweatshirts go for $75 or more. It’s definitely not a need, especially since I’ll get a very nice medal to memorialize the race. But it’s newspaper-themed, so as a journalist, I was extra (extra) enticed.

In total, this marathon has been a pricey endeavor, but hasn’t cost more than I’d spend on a regular week-long vacation. Beyond the financial investment, though, I have spent countless hours and a lot of energy on training, and for now I don’t regret any of it. Plus, the time I spent training also saved me some money I likely would have spent elsewhere.

I can’t calculate exactly how much training has saved me, but I’ve certainly declined some nights out and drinks here and there due to my running schedule. Plus spending two to three hours running — plus recovery time — on Saturdays and Sundays likely saved me from at least a few impromptu shopping trips.

There’s evidence to support the idea that regular running may help me save on healthcare costs in the long term, but it’s impossible to predict what ailments I may encounter or avoid in the future, and whether running has a direct correlation.

Training for this race has been a truly gratifying experience. I’ve spent more time outside than I regularly do, have explored more of the city I’ve called home for seven years and I’ve felt the effects of high-impact cardio training — I can confirm endorphins really do make you happy. I’m looking forward to the immense pride I’ll feel crossing the finish line on Sunday with 26.2 miles behind me.
But I have no plans to run another marathon, frankly. I know race day will be an incredible experience, but all in all, I’d rather spend my time — and money — on less intense activities.

title: Anthropic is going public—1 number from its filing is an encouraging sign for investors, says IPO expert
author: Kamaron McNair
description: Anthropic has filed to go public. Here’s what retail investors should weigh, from valuation and risks to what IPO research says about large companies.
keywords: makeit, Articles, NVIDIA Corp, Space Exploration Technologies Corp, Robinhood Markets Inc, Uber Technologies Inc, JPMorgan Chase & Co, Donald Trump, Make It, Make It - Money, Make It - Save and Invest, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence company Anthropic filed an S-1 prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, indicating it will go public in the near future. The five-year-old company behind AI assistant Claude is expected to be one of the biggest initial public offerings in history. It could take the top spot if it exceeds SpaceX’s $75 billion debut in June.

Retail investors may be excited to get a piece of what looks to be one of the big winners of the AI era. But as with any investment, they’d be wise to do some research before just buying into the hype.

Since no one can truly predict the future, there’s no certainty as to what will happen to a company’s stock price after its IPO. Anthropic in particular outlined numerous risks in its filing, including shifting regulatory and political landscapes, the existential threat of AI to humanity and the need for massive amounts of power to fuel Anthropic’s computing.

Plus, for better or worse, a company’s immediate IPO performance may not determine its long-term success. Robinhood, for example, had a fairly lackluster IPO on July 29, 2021, debuting at $38 a share. It closed that day well below opening price and fell below $7 a share in June 2022. But the stock climbed to a peak of $143 in July 2025 and closed at around $95 on Tuesday. Uber had a similar market debut in 2019, with shares falling more than 7% after its debut, but now trading about 46% higher than its initial price.

The good news for prospective Anthropic investors is that stocks with a proven sales track record have typically found their footing. From 1980 through 2024, companies that did $1 billion or more in sales in the previous 12 months have, on average, nearly matched the return of the broad stock market in the three years following their IPO, according to research by Jay Ritter, director of the IPO Initiative at the University of Florida.

“Bigger companies, as measured by sales, whether it’s $100 million or a billion, on average have pretty much matched the market,” he says. “In other words, once it starts trading, the institutional investors setting the price on average have gotten it right.”
Anthropic brought in nearly $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, according to its S-1 filing.
Still, that recent success doesn’t mean investors should go all in on a brand-new stock.

Especially with buzzy companies, it’s common for share prices to jump after the IPO. From 1980 through 2025, stocks have risen by an average of 19% from their offering price, the pre-opening price set by the offering’s underwriters, on the first day of trading, per Ritter’s analysis.

But retail investors may not reap that benefit because most offering-priced shares are typically reserved for institutional investors. Anthropic is considering offering 15% to 20% of IPO shares to retail investors through JPMorgan Chase & Co., Bloomberg reports. Anyone unable to buy at that opportunity will have to wait until shares hit the public market.
Even if Anthropic shares pop after the IPO and stay elevated for some time after, Ritter says that since the company’s valuation is already so high, “the upside is limited.”

Anthropic is reportedly aiming to go public at a valuation between $1.5 trillion to over $2 trillion. Currently, chipmaker Nvidia holds the title of most valuable public company, with a market cap — found by multiplying a stock’s share price by the number of shares outstanding — of $5.2 trillion. While Anthropic could theoretically exceed that, doing so wouldn’t offer as much upside for investors as one may hope, Ritter says.
“When you’re going public at a $1.5 trillion valuation, the possibility of making more than 10x is really limited,” he says.

There are indicators Anthropic could maintain a strong business, like the fact that its revenue is growing much faster than costs, Ritter adds. Still, as with any public company, he warns against “putting all your eggs in one basket.” He recommends making bets on any individual stock with “play money” you can afford to lose, rather than a major portion of your core portfolio. Overall, he encourages investors to keep their investment strategy boring.

His best advice for almost all investors is to buy and hold in low-cost index funds. If you do, you likely won’t even need to buy individual Anthropic shares to get some exposure to it in your portfolio. Given its potential post-IPO market size, Anthropic stock may soon be included in funds, like the Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market Fund, that aim to track the performance of the broad U.S. stock market, Ritter says.

The five-year-old company behind AI assistant Claude is expected to be one of the biggest initial public offerings in history. It could take the top spot if it exceeds SpaceX’s $75 billion debut in June.
