title: I house sit year-round and live in NYC for $800/month: 'I love the freedom this lifestyle gives me'
author: Alanna Parrish
description: 34-year-old house sitter Alanna Parrish doesn't have a permanent home and moves as many times at 8 times a month. She says she wouldn't trade it for anything.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Travel, Housing rental, Real estate, San Francisco, Lifestyle, New York, Arts and entertainment, New York City, Make It, Make It - Success, Make It - Life, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: Every time I tell someone how I live, I inevitably get the same question: “Wait, you can actually do that?”

I started house-sitting in 2023 as a way to save money while I was traveling. A year and a half ago, I decided to make New York my home base. I spend about 85% of my time here, but I’ve never paid any rent to live in the city, because I house sit all year round.

In 2026, so far, I’ve spent about $4,000 on travel expenses — including planes, trains, buses, subways and Ubers — and any fill-in accommodation I need between house sits. I pay $19 per month for my phone and spend about $75 per week on groceries. Without bills like rent, electricity or Wi-Fi, these are essentially my only consistent overhead costs. I’m spending about $800 per month.

House-sitting has completely transformed my life. I may not have a place of my own, and the structure of my calendar is unusual. But my life is rich in travel and all the wonderful people and animals I meet. To me, that’s a pretty good trade.

Four years ago, I was about to turn 30 and my life looked really different. I had a 9-to-5 role working as a project manager in a real estate office in the San Francisco Bay Area. When the pandemic hit, my steady routine was completely upended.

At first it was freeing, but after a while it just felt like I was losing time. Ready for a change, in 2022, I did what many people would probably advise against — I quit my job and bought a one-way ticket to Italy.

My plan was to live off of my savings for as long as I could. I traveled throughout Europe, Southeast Asia and Central America for two years. During that time I spent roughly $50,000. I knew that my savings would eventually run out, so I started searching for ways to travel more economically. House-sitting seemed like a real possibility.

I was back in the Bay Area and living temporarily with my family when I did my first house sit in San Francisco. I found it through TrustedHousesitters, where I still find a lot of my bookings. It lasted for three days over a long weekend and I cared for one dog. I did five local house sits before I started traveling for them.

I quickly realized that I genuinely loved taking care of people’s homes and, especially, their pets. Travel has long been a huge passion of mine, so knowing that I was helping someone else enjoy their own trip made me so happy.

If you want to become a house sitter, I also recommend starting local. It helped me get experiences and references in familiar surroundings before I jumped to places where I had to learn to do everything on the fly.

A typical house sit for me can range anywhere from two to 30 days, although my average is around one week. During periods with shorter sits, sometimes I move as many as eight times in a month. The majority of my sits — about 80% — are unpaid and in exchange for housing.

When I do charge, my fee is generally $50 to $100 per day. My bigger expenses come when my bookings don’t line up perfectly in my calendar. In the past year, I’d estimate it has happened around 10 to 12 times. When I have a gap, I have a few options. If it’s just one night, I’ll usually stay with a friend. If it’s a few nights, I might book a hotel or Airbnb. If I have a longer gap, I’ll often use it as an opportunity to travel somewhere else.

I’m definitely a budget traveler, and I’ll always look for the best deal possible. But I’m generally not willing to sacrifice too much convenience to save money. I’m not taking flights at terrible times or booking two- or three-stop itineraries just to save $50. I still want to enjoy my travels.

Even though my overhead expenses are low, there are definitely costs to doing this that don’t show up in my bank account. I love the freedom this lifestyle gives me, but it’s definitely not for everyone. The biggest trade-off is the uncertainty and the need to be flexible.

I’m constantly planning where I’m going to live next and how I’m going to get there. Moving from one home to another means that I’m always adjusting to a new space, neighborhood, gym routine, pet care routine and trash pickup days.

Sometimes I’m booked months in advance. Other times, I’m figuring things out just a few days before a house sit begins. I’ve also had to deal with last-minute cancellations and unexpected changes. I devote a lot of time to figuring out my days. I spend hours planning and doing the administrative work required to set up my next house sit and make sure my bookings line up as seamlessly as possible.
Space is also not something I take for granted. I live out of a suitcase, so I have to be incredibly selective about what I buy and what I keep.

From my years of full-time travel, I’m used to figuring out where I’m going next, how I’m going to get there and where I’m going to stay. The difference is that now, instead of paying for accommodation, I usually have a home waiting for me.

Because I’m staying in these houses often for weeks at a time, I get to explore neighborhoods, develop routines and experience places more like a local than a tourist passing through. It can be lonely at times and I have to be proactive about building community. To expand my network, I make a point to meet friends of friends, put myself in social situations and simply say yes.

To date, I have done close to 100 house sits in 22 different cities around the world. This year, I have done house sits in Edinburgh, Los Angeles, Montreal, Philadelphia, San Francisco, and, of course, New York.

I know I won’t be able to do this forever, and I would like to have a place of my own one day, but I don’t have a time frame at the moment. In the future, I would like to be able to live in two to three cities throughout the year.

In the meantime, last year, I got a remote job working as a patient support specialist for a telehealth company. I can work from anywhere, so I’m not tied to one city. The regular change of scenery keeps remote work from becoming monotonous.

I love giving people peace of mind while they’re on vacation or in another part of the world, knowing that their home is being looked after and their animals are cared for, safe and happy. It’s wild to me that something I started as a way to save money while traveling has turned into a lifestyle and career. I know it sounds unconventional, and it definitely is. But I truly love it.

Alanna Parrish is a writer and a digital nomad who has turned house- and pet-sitting into a way to travel while experiencing new places like a local. She has completed sits in more than 20 cities and has visited over 40 countries.

title: To make yourself 'unforgettable' in an AI-driven world, do these 5 counterintuitive things, says leadership expert
author: Erica Dhawan
description: "Use Your Brain" author and leadership coach Erica Dhawan shares how to stand out in an increasingly automated world.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Workplace relationships, Relationships, Artificial intelligence, Generative AI, Leadership, Science, Make It, How to Talk to People , Make It - Psychology and Relationships, Make It - Work, Make It - Success, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: It used to be that to stand out at work, we needed to be fast, polished, and agreeable. In the age of artificial intelligence, all of that gets turned on its head. Now, anyone can produce anything quickly with the appearance of poise and tact.

For nearly two decades, I’ve coached CEOs and senior executives on how to communicate, collaborate, and stand out as leaders. But over the past few years, I started noticing something troubling: the very qualities that once made people successful at work were becoming easier to automate. If everyone has access to the same intelligence, what will actually make someone unforgettable?

For my forthcoming book, “Use Your Brain,” I interviewed CEOs, scientists, artists, parents, and students across five continents. As someone who was becoming increasingly uncomfortable with my own AI use, I sought to understand what separates people who use AI to sharpen and improve their thinking from those who surrender to it and lose their point of view.
What I found was that the people who retained their autonomy and kept their work memorable had developed these counterintuitive habits.

I’ve found the best critical thinkers don’t rush. When using any AI tool, they employ what psychologist Sumona De Graaf calls a “Think Sandwich” — Think, AI, Think. To build your own “Think Sandwich,” take five minutes to answer three key questions before you prompt.

The first one forces you to develop your own point of view before AI gives you one. The second one keeps you from getting a brilliant answer to the wrong question. And the third one makes you consider the risks and consequences that a polished AI response might overlook.
Without them, you risk solving the wrong problem, accepting assumptions you never questioned or mistaking a convincing answer for a good one.

After you answer these questions, then consider using AI to review your research or first draft. You can also invite it to attack your argument or poke holes in what you wrote. But I would also get a gut check from another human being who knows the context that you are working in.
I had a coaching client, a newly promoted senior vice president at a large company, who had started letting an AI assistant draft his email replies.

A few months later, he received his annual review from his direct reports. He told me that one colleague wrote that it had become hard to tell where he stood on anything. Another said that he sounded “polished,” but didn’t frame it as a compliment.

It used to be that polish signaled credibility. Now with the proliferation of AI tools, that polish can seem cheap or empty. But being less polished doesn’t mean leaving bad grammar and typos in your work. It can look like:

This week, before you send your next important e-mail, ask yourself: “Could anyone else have written this?” If the answer is yes, look for ways to be more specific. Authenticity will resonate more than perfection.

When everyone has access to tools that validate their thinking, we risk creating workplaces where assumptions go unchallenged and bad ideas sound brilliant. That makes healthy disagreement at work more important, not less.
The people who stand out will be the ones who are willing to challenge the thinking in the room, including their own.
Here’s how to go looking for disagreement in a constructive and helpful way:

These habits make disagreement feel less like a personal attack and more like a shared effort to get to a better answer. Questions lower defensiveness, finding common ground builds trust, and inviting criticism makes it safer for others to speak up.

When I ask executives who they believe are the most at risk of handing their thinking to AI, they usually point to Gen Z or junior employees. The irony is that I see the opposite in my coaching work. This is because executives’ roles have shifted from doing the work to reviewing it. Now AI makes that review process even easier, serving up polished summaries, recommendations and decisions in seconds.

The danger is that leaders who spend all their time just approving answers then struggle to identify biases in their team’s work. This leads to A-level work on the surface, with C-level understanding of the issue at hand.
The higher you rise, the more consequential that loss of independent judgment becomes. To intentionally protect their thought processes, I recommend that leaders:

If your message contains emotion, conflict, disagreement or requires a hard decision, pick up the phone or organize an in-person meeting to have a real-time conversation. Don’t just show up to deliver your message. Start by asking a question you genuinely don’t know the answer to and listen without planning your response or rushing to a bot.

Pay attention to what’s not being said, whether that is hesitation, a change in tone, or a concern someone seems reluctant to raise. Before concluding the meeting, make sure the other person feels heard by echoing what matters most to them.

I’ve found that the conversations people remember aren’t necessarily the ones where you said something brilliant. They’re the ones where you made someone feel understood, challenged their thinking with care or had the courage to say what needed to be said.
AI can help you craft the perfect message, but it can’t replace the trust that you personally build in the moment.

Erica Dhawan is a leadership expert, keynote speaker, and Wall Street Journal bestselling author of “Digital Body Language” and “Get Big Things Done.” Her new book, “Use Your Brain: Think Deeper in a World on Autopilot,” is out Jan. 12, 2027.

title: I quit my marketing job to walk dogs for 4 months: It's 'one of the most valuable professional experiences I've ever had'
author: Sally Simmons
description: "People sometimes assume dog walking was a gap or detour in my career. I see it as one of the most valuable professional experiences I've had," says Sally Simmons.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Marketing, Dogs, California, Arts and entertainment, Lifestyle, Kentucky, Make It, Make It - Success, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: One early morning in 2022, I found myself watching a dog walker on TikTok and thinking: I want her job.
It felt ridiculous. I was finishing up my MBA and navigating the next chapter of my career with a focus on prestige and financial success.

But soon after relocating from Kentucky to California in October 2021, I burned out. I had transitioned into a remote healthcare marketing role, living on the West Coast but still working East Coast hours and completing my second year of business school from afar. While everyone around me seemed to be heading to the beach and enjoying the sunshine, I spent my days inside, glued to a computer screen.
The dog walker I followed online seemed to have everything I was craving: fresh air, movement, flexibility and a job that didn’t revolve around emails and Zoom meetings.
During a long drive, I joked with my husband, “I think I’m going to quit my job and walk dogs.” The joke quickly became a plan.

Within the span of just a few weeks in the spring of 2022, I quit my job, graduated from business school, traveled to Europe for an old roommate’s wedding and then flew to Texas to speak at the Latino Franchise Symposium. While I was there, I created my Rover profile. I highlighted my experience volunteering at animal shelters in college, pet sitting for friends and caring for animals throughout my life.
Before I even made it back home to California, I had my first meet-and-greet scheduled with a potential client. Shortly after, I landed my first booking. I was thrilled.

At first, I intentionally priced my services below what seemed typical in my area to build reviews, charging about $15 for a drop-in visit and about $17 for a 30-minute walk. Some days I had just one client. I was able to start small because I had savings to tide me over, along with a partner whose job provided steady income and benefits.
Still, I treated it like a real business from day one. I accepted nearly every opportunity that came my way, taking dogs on midday walks, housesitting on weekends and boarding dogs in my apartment.

I sent thoughtful updates to the dog owners filled with photos, detailed notes and plenty of emojis. I shared bathroom break tallies, funny moments and anything unusual they should know. If I stayed overnight, I brought in packages, cleaned up after myself and made sure their home looked exactly as they had left it.
My goal wasn’t simply to complete the booking. It was to become the person people trusted with a member of their family.

The reviews started rolling in. As my profile gained traction, I gradually increased my rates, eventually charging $23 for a drop-in visit and $84 for overnight stays. By the time I left the platform four months later, I had earned a five-star rating with 30 reviews, built a roster of recurring clients and filled my calendar.

One of my favorite memories came when a family asked me to care for their dogs during their wedding weekend. I spent two and a half days at a beautiful resort and dressed the dogs in tiny tuxedos before they walked down the aisle.

It reminded me that this work was about helping families enjoy some of the biggest moments of their lives with peace of mind. Years later, we’re still friends. They now have a daughter, and my daughter and I recently attended her first birthday party.

Some days I walked more than eight miles, logging over 18,000 steps as I explored neighborhoods I otherwise never would have discovered. I spent hours outside instead of sitting behind a desk. Sometimes I listened to podcasts or music. Other times, I simply enjoyed the quiet.
Those walks gave me space to think. I reflected on what success actually meant, what I wanted my career to look like and, perhaps more importantly, how I wanted my days to feel.

Before Rover, success meant getting promotions, landing bigger clients and climbing the corporate ladder. Walking dogs challenged that definition. I realized I didn’t want to chase an impressive title as much as I wanted to chase a lifestyle that gave me energy.
Ironically, it was during one of those walks that I received the phone call offering me the marketing job I still have today. I paused on the sidewalk, accepted the offer and then finished the walk.

Returning to marketing wasn’t a difficult decision. By then, I was pregnant with my first daughter and needed the stability, benefits and predictable income that came with a full-time role. When an excited dog chasing a squirrel pulled me to the ground early in my pregnancy, it became clear that my season as a professional dog walker was coming to an end.
Still, I think about those four months often. People sometimes assume dog walking was a gap or detour in my career. I see it as one of the most valuable professional experiences I’ve ever had.

It reminded me that passion is visible, no matter what kind of work you’re doing. It reinforced that the skills that matter most — showing up, listening, caring deeply, building trust and making small, consistent changes — translate to every career.

And even though I’m back in marketing, my days look different than they did before my dog-walking era. These days, you’ll find me logging off at 5 p.m. to go play outside with my family before dinner, walking near the ocean after a hard week, having kitchen dance parties to shake off the day, taking calls while walking my own dog or squeezing in a lunchtime workout. The fresh air and sense of presence give me the balance I craved when I was glued to screens on a schedule dictated by someone else’s time zone.

Those four months taught me something my MBA never could: Success isn’t just about finding a job that sounds impressive. It’s about building a life you genuinely enjoy living, even if it doesn’t look like the one you originally imagined.

Sally Simmons is a marketing leader and holistic health coach based in California. After years building strategies for global brands, she found unexpected lessons about business, connection and success during a four-month chapter as a professional dog walker. Today, she brings those lessons into her work helping people create healthier, more balanced lives.

title: In the wake of Weil, a legal recruiter's advice for surviving a company wind-down
author: Danielle Thompson
description: Legal recruiter Danielle Thompson shares her best advice for the employees of Weil, Gotshal & Manges and others who face a company wind-down or dissolution.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Personnel, Labor economy, United States, Make It, Make It - Work, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: It’s hard to believe a corporate giant like Weil, Gotshal & Manges — a top 20 U.S. law firm that reportedly had over $2 billion in revenue in 2025 — could move toward ceasing operations just like that. But occasionally a Weil-like wind-down — or even a collapse like Lehman Brothers, Silicon Valley Bank or FTX — is bound to occur.
And here we are, seeing a major law firm move toward shutting down in real time.

The firm’s management committee recommended that its partners prepare to close its doors after more than 90 years in business, Weil, Gotshal & Manges said on Wednesday. “Following a careful review of strategic alternatives, the Firm’s Management Committee has recommended to the partnership that the Firm pursue an orderly wind-down,” the firm said in a statement to CNBC on Wednesday. “The partners are expected to vote in the coming days.”

As a legal recruiter and former big law associate, I’m here to provide practical insights to the employees, lawyers and non-lawyers alike, who’ve just learned they’re about to be out of a job — and those who are scared their company might be next.

First, let’s be clear: From where I stand, Weil is an anomaly. But when a company does make headlines for winding down, or failing and shutting down, it’s rarely the employees whose plight is highlighted: the people whose careers have been destabilized, whose anxiety shoots through the roof and who become the collateral damage of business decisions they had no idea were being made until far too late.

Here are my top tips, for both lawyers and non-lawyers, for when your company announces or is headed toward dissolution. In the case of Weil, it’s advice I hope the firm’s roughly 1,200 lawyers plus staff take to heart in the next 90 days.
Yes, you can worry. Yes, you can grieve. But you should also mobilize quickly.

A lot of Weil associates are in a holding pattern right now: either waiting to see where their favorite partners are going and hoping they offer to bring them along, or thinking 90 days of pay, as reported by Reuters, means they have 90 days in which to start looking.

While many associates will eventually follow their partners, I suggest looking for a new job on your own while you wait. The market is absolutely inundated with Weil associates right now, on top of everyone else whose firm isn’t dissolving but was already looking to make a lateral move. You don’t want to be late to the party and find all your peers are ahead of you in line.

Partners are also under no obligation to bring you with them, and you have no say in where they choose to go. There’s no guarantee it would be a good fit for you. It’s best to have options and it’s comforting to feel like you have some control over those options, especially in such uncertain times.

I’d give similar advice to non-lawyers. Don’t wait too long. Options are always good. Be proactive. The people who tend to come out of these situations the least scathed are the ones who start looking before any announcement is made, in cases where the writing’s on the wall and everyone else is still hoping for a last-minute save.
Even as you move fast, try to be cautious. You don’t want to be taken advantage of.

Just this week, I’ve counseled about a dozen Weil associates to do their homework, however quickly, before blasting their resume to every firm and recruiter on the block. Some recruiters — especially in the legal industry — will take you sending your resume as blanket consent to submit you anywhere they like.

But from what I’ve seen working in legal recruiting, if more than one recruiter sends your materials to the same firm, you’re very unlikely to ever hear from that firm again. They see it as sloppy, bad form and too much of a headache to manage the inevitable fight over who’s entitled to the hypothetical fee for your placement.

So keep a firm grasp on where your resume is at all times. You should know exactly which companies have it and who they got it from. If you plan to use a recruiter, pick a reputable and trusted one. Don’t race to the first recruiter who cold calls you or the last recruiter in your inbox. Instead, get referrals from friends, set up intro calls with multiple recruiters to get a vibe check, pick one and only send that one your resume.

For non-legal folks, recruiting may not be so cutthroat. But I still recommend caution regarding how and where you share your information. Focus on trusted connections, including verifiable HR professionals at your target companies, friend and colleague referrals, your college career services office and known job boards. Be wary of answering outreach from questionable sources.
A short unemployment stint won’t kill your career, and neither will multiple moves in quick succession.

When the unexpected occurs and the resulting job market frenzy ensues, sometimes, even when you mobilize early and wisely, you won’t land a new job right away. Perhaps the only upside to the mass publicity of these surprise dissolutions is that every prospective employer is going to take one look at your resume and understand why you’re out of work. They won’t wonder what you did wrong, whether you got fired or if you’re qualified.

But those favorable assumptions don’t last forever. I’d give it one to six months. That’s another plug for not waiting until a dissolution date to start your search, especially in the current job market, where as of September 27.1% of those who are unemployed have been searching for over six months, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Keep in mind too that job decisions made in haste or with your back against a wall are much more likely to end in a mismatch. Most people will take the first offer they get. Some will accept an unsustainable commute or a tyrant of a boss for short-term job security. And if it’s your only option, that might be the right decision for you — we all have bills to pay and mouths to feed.

If that’s the case, know it’s also okay to move on quickly. I don’t begrudge anyone who makes a job decision out of necessity and then course corrects when they’re out of survival mode. And from my experience as a recruiter, neither will most future employers.

None of this is your fault and all of it is horribly unfair. It’s okay if you’re feeling angry, terrified, overwhelmed, frozen, devastated or even a little relieved. Whatever you’re feeling, both in the immediate aftermath and in the weeks and months after, is completely valid. Give yourself ample space and grace for whatever comes up and seek help and support.

On the flip side, lend a helping hand wherever you can, especially once you find a job, which I believe you will. Pay it forward by helping others who are still looking or looking again. Share a good resource, refer them to a trusted recruiter and connect them to any job opportunities you’ve passed up or heard about.
Corporations don’t have feelings or loyalty to any given employee. But people do. We are nothing without our empathy and our communities. Hard times are when we need both the most.

Danielle Thompson is a legal recruiter and former big law employment lawyer based in the Bay Area. A managing director at Damato Search Group, she holds a J.D. from Columbia Law School and a B.A., magna cum laude, from UC Santa Barbara.

title: AI-driven layoffs are creating a new class of boomerang employees—companies are realizing they 'pulled the plug too quickly'
author: Sophie Caldwell
description: Some companies are quietly rehiring workers they laid off due to AI, according to a recent report from SHL.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Labor economy, Personnel, Ford Motor Co, Amazon.com Inc, United States, Make It, Make It - Work, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: AI-driven layoffs dominated the headlines this year.
Employers cited AI as the primary reason for almost 40% of the job cuts announced in May 2026, according to a report from outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.
But new research shows that some employers may be rethinking those job cuts and reversing course in a trend experts call “AI rebounding.”

In a survey of more than 1,000 U.S. workers, nearly 1 in 5 respondents say that they have been laid off or replaced by AI and then asked to return, according to a recent report from SHL, a talent acquisition and talent management company. The survey, which SHL commissioned from market research firm Propeller Insights, also polled over 1,000 U.K. workers. It was conducted between June and July 2026 and had a margin of error of 5%.

These findings indicate that companies are realizing they “pulled the plug too quickly” on their human employees, according to Lucy Beaumont, global senior vice president of product and design at SHL.

Several large employers like Ford and Amazon have reversed course after enacting AI-related layoffs in the past year. A March report by Orgvue found that 32% of organizations that let workers go due to AI have had to rehire staff.
It’s a mistake for companies to approach AI implementation as if it were any other software rollout, says Joseph Fuller, professor of management practice at Harvard Business School.

From a company’s perspective, “in order to spend money on a new technology, we have to find some savings in the budget, and the way we’ve done that with previous technology deployments is by laying people off.”

But AI is most useful when it’s linked with a human worker’s “contextual intelligence,” i.e. their background knowledge and understanding of an issue, he says: “The more you know about important processes, the more value you can extract from the AI.”
AI can’t fully replace “people that know the business, that know their customers, that have judgment, that can bring empathy, that have that human connection,” Beaumont says.
Most workers are open to returning after a layoff: only 6.6% of U.S. workers say they would refuse to come back under any circumstances, according to the SHL study.
But those who do return are “going to be a lot more demanding of what they expect from an employer,” Beaumont says.

According to SHL’s research, almost half of surveyed U.S. workers would require a significant pay increase to return to their roles, and 43% would want “written guarantees” of job security. A similar number, 40%, would require “full transparency” regarding how AI would be used in their role before they’d rejoin the company. And 30% of workers say that an apology or acknowledgment from leadership is a key condition of their return.
Above all, employees are looking for reassurance, Beaumont says: “How do I know that this isn’t going to happen again?”

Even when workers do return, employers need to understand that company morale is going to take a hit, according to Beaumont. Being laid off “fundamentally changes” the psychological contract between employer and employee, she says, and being rehired isn’t enough to repair that relationship.
“You’ve really broken the trust with those people,” Beaumont says.

As a result, returning workers are unlikely to have the same levels of “productivity and engagement” as they did before a layoff, she says. “Culture is so difficult to change, and once you’ve impacted it negatively, it’s so difficult to recover from.”

To stay relevant in the job market, employees are prioritizing skill development, Beaumont says: U.S. survey respondents say that they’re teaching themselves how to use AI tools (44%), developing industry-specific skills that can’t be easily replicated by AI (42.6%), working on interpersonal and leadership skills (40%) and honing creative and strategic thinking (38%).

Given how quickly AI’s capabilities will grow, the most important skill for employees to hone is adaptability, Fuller says. He urges workers to practice working with AI regularly and “seek out opportunities” to upskill with the technology.

Workers will also need to get comfortable with change, he says. In the near future, Fuller predicts that AI will create “permanent tumult” within many organizations as they continue to recalibrate their staffing needs around AI advancements.

Beaumont recommends that workers identify the areas where their unique skills can have the most impact: “If AI is going to take away some of those easily automated tasks, what’s left for me to do, and how can I optimize the human side that I can bring?”

Leaders should focus on questions like, “What kind of upskilling do people need? What new opportunities are there for people? What kind of internal mobility am I opening up as a result of AI?” she says.
The organizations that will be successful are the ones who “are using AI to optimize what they do,” Beaumont says — not just to cut costs.

	Given how quickly AI’s capabilities will grow, the most important skill for employees to hone is adaptability, Fuller says. He urges workers to practice working with AI regularly and “seek out opportunities” to upskill with the technology.
	Workers will also need to get comfortable with change, he says. In the near future, Fuller predicts that AI will create “permanent tumult” within many organizations as they continue to recalibrate their staffing needs around AI advancements.
	Beaumont recommends that workers identify the areas where their unique skills can have the most impact: “If AI is going to take away some of those easily automated tasks, what’s left for me to do, and how can I optimize the human side that I can bring?”
	Leaders should focus on questions like, “What kind of upskilling do people need? What new opportunities are there for people? What kind of internal mobility am I opening up as a result of AI?” she says.
	The organizations that will be successful are the ones who “are using AI to optimize what they do,” Beaumont says — not just to cut costs.

title: Workers and researchers see benefits in GLP-1 access. Companies are weighing the costs
author: Jennifer Liu, Juhohn Lee
description: As GLP-1 use reaches new highs, more employers are grappling with whether the benefits of covering these medications justify their high costs.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Health, Weight loss, Weight loss drugs, Labor economy, Social issues, Walmart Inc, Bank of America Corp, Medication, Personnel, United States, Make It, Make It - Work, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: Kristi Kennebrew knows firsthand how transformative GLP-1 medications can be — and just how much getting employer coverage for them can make or break a budget.

Kennebrew began taking Mounjaro in December 2022, which was covered 100% by her employer at the time, and says she went from weighing about 265 pounds down to 185 over about a year. The weight loss helped her feel more confident, more social and more energetic, she says.

She lost coverage at the beginning of 2024 after she was let go from her job, so she went cold turkey until she got a prescription in early 2025 for another drug to the tune of $399 per month. Finally, in the fall of 2025, Kennebrew landed a new job in recruitment marketing. Her employer-sponsored health insurance covers GLP-1s under a coaching program, and she pays just $25 out of pocket monthly.
Working for a company that covers the majority of her GLP-1 costs “provides comfort,” Kennebrew, 31, of Dallas tells CNBC Make It.
Some 11% of U.S. adults say they’re currently taking a GLP-1 medication specifically for weight loss in 2026, up from 3% in 2024, according to Gallup.

Employer-sponsored insurance is the largest source of health coverage for Americans under 65, covering more than 165 million people in March 2025. For millions of workers, whether their insurance covers a GLP-1 can depend largely on their employer.

Some companies are embracing it. Walmart plans to cover more than 250 prescription medications, including GLP-1s for diabetes, at no cost to its employees in 2027, while Bank of America is spending more than $250 million a year to provide GLP-1 weight loss meds to its workforce.

Others are scaling back: An early 2026 survey of 105 employer members of the nonprofit Business Group on Health found that while two-thirds of them were covering GLP-1s for weight management, 10% of those companies said they would likely drop that coverage in 2027.
As GLP-1 use reaches new highs, employers are grappling with whether the benefits of covering these medications justify their high costs.

Companies that cover these meds could have an advantage. According to a December survey of 545 workers from virtual health clinic 9amHealth, a majority of workers, 73%, said GLP-1 coverage was an important factor for taking or staying at a job, and 31% would change jobs to gain coverage.

Several people who spoke with Make It say taking weight loss medications has a number of benefits: Better sleep, more energy and sharper focus with less food noise that makes them obsess over food. Others say the physical changes also give them a confidence boost that motivates them to chase new opportunities they wouldn’t have otherwise.
When it comes to the workplace, early research suggests GLP-1 use could affect who gets hired.

One working paper by Harvard economist Rebecca Diamond, which hasn’t been peer reviewed, found women who were unemployed increased their likelihood of landing a job by 26.9 percentage points after 18 months of taking a GLP-1, compared with women who wanted to take the medication but hadn’t.

Women who were already working didn’t appear to work more hours or gain new promotions after starting GLP-1s. One possible factor may be that weight bias makes a bigger difference when employers are making hiring decisions and forming first impressions than when evaluating workers they already know.

Weight stigma in the workplace tends to be more pronounced for women than for men, says Rebecca Puhl, a distinguished professor in the department of human development and family sciences at the University of Connecticut.

“In our society, thinness has come to symbolize very strong values” like self-discipline, willpower and motivation, Puhl says. “And if people have a higher body weight that doesn’t conform to those ideals, they can be negatively stereotyped as lacking in those characteristics.”
“Employers are not immune to those broader societal attitudes,” she says, and “those assumptions can influence hiring decisions.”

Kennebrew in Dallas says her weight has fluctuated over the years while on different GLP-1 drugs. It can be tough to acknowledge, but she says she felt “at her prime” at her lowest weight, and that she got more requests to appear at conferences or do public speaking events at a smaller size.
“Not only was I smaller, but I was a lot more confident in myself too,” she says. “I don’t know if I would have felt as confident or really [been] picked for that opportunity if I was bigger.”

Scott Schilling says dropping 38 pounds since starting a GLP-1 in April helped him confront both weight bias and ageism at work. Schilling, 68, of Dallas was recently interviewing for new sales jobs and recalls being told that he was more energetic than his interviewers expected him to be.
“The mental side of releasing the weight and moving forward again reinvigorates you to be able to take on the world at the time where the world has not made it easy for those over 50,” he says.

GLP-1 use may help workers spend less time away from their jobs. Another recent working paper published in July by the National Bureau of Economic Research looked at patients taking GLP-1s in Denmark. Given the medication’s ability to improve metabolic and cardiovascular health and provide other benefits, researchers were interested in whether GLP-1 use could improve “work capacity” and impact the labor market, says Jonathan Zhang, assistant professor of public policy at Duke University.

Researchers found in that working paper that GLP-1 treatment for weight loss reduced long-term sickness leave, defined as illness-related absences lasting more than 30 days, by 17.3%. That could have big economic consequences. In Denmark, the reduced sick leave saved employers and the public sector the equivalent of about $722 per year for each employed person receiving treatment.
Meanwhile, chronic diseases, including diabetes, which GLP-1 medications can treat, are projected to cost the U.S. an average of $900 billion annually in lost employee productivity.
There are some caveats: The research findings apply to Denmark and may not translate directly to the U.S. “It’s a bit of a speculation,” Zhang says.

GLP-1 users are already rearranging their spending to make room for health costs. Roughly half, 51%, of current GLP-1 users worry they may have to choose between their meds and saving enough for retirement, while others have taken on debt, pulled money from savings or cut their retirement contributions to cover the cost of these medications, according to an October report from Nationwide Retirement Institute.

Many users are making room for the costs now but may not be able to keep it up in the long term. Megan Tuano in Pittsburgh began taking Zepbound in August and has paid for her $300 monthly doses (after a coupon) out of pocket, as her insurance doesn’t cover it and neither did her husband’s. He was recently laid off and is now looking for a new role. Tuano says they’re paying closer attention to whether prospective employers offer any coverage for weight loss drugs. They’d take lower paying jobs if they had more comprehensive health insurance coverage in general, including for coverage of GLP-1 meds, Tuano says.
“What stands out to me most is access,” Tuano says. “If these medications do open doors, it worries me that the people who could benefit most may be the ones who can’t afford them.”

So far, studies haven’t established that GLP-1 treatments pay for themselves through lower medical spending in the short term. Employers, meanwhile, are trying to figure out if it’s worth the high cost to cover GLP-1s for their employees. Some are reconsidering their coverage.

In a March survey, nearly eight in 10 employers told Business Group on Health that GLP-1s are driving an increase in their company’s healthcare costs. The average employer-provided family health insurance plan cost $28,303 in 2026, up by 5% from a year ago, according to an October report from KFF, a health policy nonprofit. Insurance cost per employee is expected to rise 8.2% on average in 2027, according to a Marsh survey of over 1,800 U.S. employers from the summer, with GLP-1 use accounting for a full percentage point of the overall increase.

“This market’s changed so quickly in the past year that we should expect it to continue to change” with pricing changes and new drugs on the horizon, says Paul Fronstin, director of health benefits research at the Employee Benefit Research Institute. “On the one hand, you could argue that as the prices come down, employers are going to be more likely to cover it. But on the other hand, the genie’s already out of the bottle in terms of a lot of workers already paying for this out of their own pocket.”

Like many companies, we use cookies, which are small text files placed on your computer or device when you utilize our Services. Strictly Necessary: These Cookies are required for Service functionality, including for system administration, delivering requested content and features, security and fraud prevention, to identify and fix technical issues, authenticate your identity, and to enable purchasing capabilities. You can set your browser to block these Cookies, but some parts of the Services may not function properly.

Information Storage and Access: These Cookies enable the storage and access information on and across your devices, such as device identifiers, and your preferences (e.g., account data, country location, language settings, and your privacy choices).

Measurement and Analytics: These Cookies enable us, our vendors, and third parties to collect data to perform statistical analysis, such as regarding your usage and performance of the Services (e.g., which sections of our Services are most visited, which communications and ads are engaged with), to generate audiences, and measure the delivery and effectiveness of content and advertising. Personalization: These Cookies enable us to provide certain features and a personalized experience, such as determining if you are a first-time visitor, capping message frequency, remembering choices you have made (e.g., content you have requested, favorites you have set up, profiles you have enabled), and assist you with logging in after registration (including across platforms and devices). Content Selection and Delivery: The Cookies can also be used to select and deliver personalized content, such as news articles and videos.

Ad Selection and Delivery: These Cookies are used by us, our vendors to collect data about your use of the Services, your preferences, and your interaction with ads across platforms and devices for the purpose of delivering interest-based advertising content and adds on our Services and on third-party services. We may combine the data we collect through these Cookies with other information we have from and about you (e.g., your account data) for these purposes.

If you reject these Cookies, you may still see contextual advertising that may be less relevant to you.

Social media platforms have the ability to track your online activity outside of the Services. This may impact the content and messages you see on other services.
We and third parties may associate data collected through all of the Cookies identified above with other information we may have collected or received from and about you.

title: Ask these questions before traveling with a partner, friend or relative: 'It'll save you time, money and disappointment'
author: Anna Goldfarb, Nell Wulfhart
description: Consider budget, accommodations, personal habits, alone time and more, say Anna Goldfarb and Nell McShane Wulfhart, experts in friendship, travel and decision-making.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Friendships, Travel, Lifestyle, Personal finance, Arts and entertainment, Make It, Make It - Psychology and Relationships, Make It - Life, Make It - Food, Travel and Tech, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: Blow-up fights at the Colosseum, tears atop Mount Kilimanjaro and clashes over the window seat: Incompatible travel buddies can ruin a vacation.

As experts in friendship, travel and decision-making, we know that the stresses and complications of travel, not to mention the near-infinite number of decisions you have to make, can put a lot of pressure on a relationship that was perfectly delightful within a 10-mile radius of your homes. There’s a reason that people tell you to travel with someone before you marry them!

Thirty-five percent of travelers found that they weren’t compatible with a travel buddy, according to a Booking.com survey conducted in July of 1,253 U.S. adults who’d gone away overnight within the last 12 months. Twenty-one percent of respondents had even left a trip part-way through because of their travel partner, and a bad vacation made 28% think about ending the relationship or friendship with their ill-suited travel companion.

The problem is that we can have different, unsaid expectations of what a getaway might entail: Does one person want every day booked dawn-to-dusk with activities, while the other wants to lounge in the hotel spa until cocktail hour? Does someone want to go all out with seafood towers and Champagne, while the rest of the group prefers to nosh on convenience store hot dogs and guzzle local beer?
Not every friend, romantic partner or family member is the right travel partner for you. And it’ll save you time, money and disappointment to figure that out before you plan your itinerary.
We’ve created a quiz to help you quickly determine compatibility with your prospective travel partner so you can sidestep potential headaches down the line.
Here are six of the most important questions:

Start with the basics. Some of us can conk out in the middle of the nightclub; others need a white noise machine, blackout curtains and a room to ourselves. The hotels, hostels or apartments you visit on your trip are key to compatibility on the road — it’s hard to have a blissful holiday when you’re exhausted from someone else’s snoring.

The carry-on vs. checked luggage debate will never die, and this is one difference it’s wise to hash out in advance. No one wants to spend days carefully choosing their most stain-resistant T-shirts to tuck into a backpack only to see the other person arrive at the check-in desk with two maxed-out suitcases. This doesn’t have to be a holiday dealbreaker, but discuss it so everyone knows what to expect.

Is your dream vacation full of leisurely days, wandering around, popping into shops and cafes that look interesting and taking afternoon naps? Or is your dream vacation full of museums, restaurants, activities and movement?

For some people, a “vacation” means downtime, with few planned activities and lots of white space to do whatever feels appealing in the moment. For others, there’s no point in leaving home unless you’re going to maximize your time, and leaving a destination without visiting every dot on your dense Google Map is a wasted holiday.

This might seem insignificant, but more than one trip has been strained by a long morning routine. One person is straightening their hair and gluing on eyelashes; the other is wearing the same outfit they had on yesterday and tapping their foot, impatiently waiting to get going.

If you’re incompatible on this point but still want to travel together, we suggest deciding on a strategy in advance. Maybe it’s okay for one person to go out and explore, get coffee or eat the hotel breakfast alone, or the traveler who takes longer to get ready commits to setting an alarm for 45 minutes before their companion.
Do you prefer to travel on the cheap? Or do you not get out of bed for fewer than five stars? In the Booking.com survey, 35% of respondents had argued over money with their travel buddy.

Budget considerations might be the most important thing to discuss before committing to anything. Ideally, you’d each set a budget for the trip, a number you’d be entirely comfortable spending, and then compare to see how far apart you are.

If one person is dreaming of an airport limousine pickup and the other person is planning to squirrel away bread rolls from the hotel breakfast to eat for lunch, you might be better off on different trips.

Ever been stuck in an airplane seat next to someone who just won’t shut up? Compatible travel isn’t just about similar taste in food and accommodations. You’re going to be spending a lot of time with your travel buddy.

So before you get on that airport shuttle, have a quick chat: Are we both okay with doing our own thing during the tedious parts of the journey? Or does one of you expect that you’ll be “on” 24 hours a day and get their feelings hurt if the other prefers to zone out to a podcast?
Once each potential traveler has answered the questions, review them together, discuss and make a decision about traveling together — or not.

Anna Goldfarb is a friendship expert and author of ”Modern Friendship: How to Nurture Our Most Valued Connections,” a Next Big Idea Club Must-Read. She writes the Substack Friendship Explained. She’s been featured in the New York Times, The Atlantic, The Washington Post, WIRED, Oprah Daily, Goop and more. Follow her on Instagram.

Nell Wulfhart has been helping people make big (and small!) decisions since 2013. Her clients have included politicians, hedge fund managers, Netflix executives, poets, parents, med students and many more. You can listen in on her coaching sessions on her podcast, The Decision Coach. Find her at decisioncoach.com.

title: Fact vs. fiction: Doctors share whether peptides are safe and effective
author: Renée Onque
description: As peptides gain popularity among some wellness influencers and federal government officials, doctors share what you need to know.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Social issues, Arts and entertainment, Science, Medication, United States, Make It, Make It - Life, Health Tips and Wellness Advice, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: From YouTube influencers to Reddit threads, the health and wellness side of the internet is full of talk about peptides.

The term refers to a class of chemical compounds made up of short chains of amino acids. In the wellness market, synthetic peptides are often sold to consumers as injectables, which some health influencers say can bring a wide range of health benefits from muscle recovery and longevity to improved sexual function. Some peptides, including GLP-1 drugs commonly used for weight loss or diabetes, are heavily researched and federally approved for medical use. Many other forms of peptides are not.

Yet even some lightly researched peptides may be on their way to pharmacy shelves. The Department of Health and Human Services is reportedly planning to allow specialty pharmacies to compound certain synthetic peptides that have the support of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who told podcaster Joe Rogan that he is a “big fan” of the injectables in a February 2026 interview. As reported, the move would be an interim access policy covering some specific peptides not currently approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

Such a move would be controversial from a regulatory point of view: Multiple peptides, including one of the compounds reportedly included in the health department’s proposal, appear on an FDA list of injectables that “may present significant safety risks.” That compound, known as BPC-157, has shown potential anti-inflammatory effects in some animal and lab studies but has not yet been subject to large-scale human testing for safety or effectiveness.

“There are a few reasons why, but one of the main ones is the absence of evidence,” including robust human studies on safety and effectiveness, says Dr. Caleb Alexander, a professor of epidemiology and medicine at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.

Yet consumer interest and regulatory momentum for peptides are growing. So here’s what you need to know about peptides, from why they’re the subject of such conversation to whether or not they’re safe or effective to use.
Peptides are “kind of like the building blocks of proteins,” says Dr. Alison Dempsey, a dermatologist at the Weill Cornell Medicine and NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital.

Several different types of peptides are naturally found in the body, like insulin and endorphins. Peptides can also be synthesized in labs, according to Harvard Health Publishing. GLP-1s, like Ozempic, are FDA-approved synthetic peptides, Dempsey says.

Injectable variations of synthetic peptides that haven’t been approved by the FDA — such as BPC-157 and GHK-Cu, the latter of which has been marketed as a potential anti-aging drug — are the peptides that are making headlines at the moment, says Dr. Pieter Cohen, an associate professor at Harvard Medical School and internist at Cambridge Health Alliance.

One likely factor behind synthetic peptides gaining more attention has been the success of drugs like Ozempic at addressing health concerns such as obesity and diabetes, according to Cohen. “That probably opened up [the idea that] there must be this magical world of these other peptides that we can have access to, that will do these sort of similar magical things in other areas,” he says.

However, Cohen and other health experts have their concerns. After all, a compound’s status as a peptide “doesn’t mean it’s close to Ozempic in any way, shape or form ... in terms of both its chemical structure or its effects on the human body,” says Cohen.

Synthetic peptides advertised on social media and sold on the so-called gray market — often produced by overseas sellers and sold to U.S. consumers outside the normal American drug regulatory system — come with marketing claims such as boosting longevity, improving sleep quality, strengthening the immune system and even enhancing skin health and sexual function, according to Alexander.

Particularly among the people who consider GLP-1s a form of miracle drug, consumers may simply want to believe that the weight loss medicine’s chemical cousins could have similar effects on other elements of human health. “Unfortunately, when it comes to peptides marketing, word of mouth has strongly surpassed where we are with any type of research,” Dempsey says.

The health experts who spoke with CNBC Make It recommend against using any injectable peptides that aren’t approved by the FDA, especially if you’re unsure where or how they were produced. Always consult with a medical professional before making any major changes that can affect your health.

“My recommendation is not to use any of the novel, unstudied injectable peptides because we simply do not know if they work. And if they do work, if they’re safe,” Cohen says. When buying peptides on the gray market, you can receive entirely different compounds or doses, and some may be contaminated with bacteria or other concerning materials, he says.
“There’s concerns both about the potential risks, but also about the unclear level of benefit from these products,” Alexander says.

“We have a great regulatory system governing prescription drugs in the United States,” Alexander adds. “For advocates of these products that really believe in them, I hope that they’ll put their money where their mouth is, and do the studies that are necessary so that we can understand the true safety and effectiveness of the products.”

title: College campuses have (largely) gone silent. Can practicing small talk and phone-free spaces change that?
author: Gili Malinsky
description: College students are spending less time socializing, which has implications for later in life and the workplace.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Education, Chicago, Make It, Make It - Life, Make It - Psychology and Relationships, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: Charlie Harker had high hopes for college.

Before starting her freshman year in 2023, the Lebanon, Ohio, resident had planned to meet people through clubs or at the dorms. She’d expected there would be an open, vibrant atmosphere ripe for making friends. She’d quickly find her people.

“And then I got to school,” says the 21-year-old senior at the University of Cincinnati. “I didn’t know anyone on my floor. No one had their door open. No one would really talk to you.” That fun and peer-filled campus life she’d been promised by both family and pop culture turned out to be, at least to some extent, a relic of the past.

Harker’s college experience is fairly common these days. From 2003 to 2025, 20-to 24-year-olds’ socializing and communicating in the U.S dropped 52%, from an average of 64 minutes per day in their leisure time to an average of just over 30 minutes per day. Over the same period, 15-to 19-year-olds’ leisure time socializing dropped 32% to 38 minutes, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Students these days view school as more “transactional” than in the past, says Steven Rogelberg, Chancellor’s professor of organizational science, management and psychology at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte. “You go there, you take your classes, and then you leave.”

That’s a problem for a variety of reasons. If they’re not meeting in class or stopping each other in the hallways, young people may be missing out on developing both friendships and social skills, which are critical for long-term life and career success. Making small talk, for instance, can help forge both personal and professional relationships down the line, says Kristie Patten, dean of NYU’s Steinhardt School of Culture, Education, and Human Development.

Also essential: building confidence, which can come both from successfully navigating social situations and making painful mistakes. Without that practice, both campus and life can become more insular and sterile.

“Parents and school systems, and maybe even legislators, are going to have to deal with this if we want a future where we have kids and adults who understand how to be social with one another,” says Lance Garrison, dean of the College of Professional Psychology at The Chicago School.
“The trajectory we are on right now is one toward increasing isolation, increasing loneliness, increasing anxiety.”

Some students and schools are tackling their campus antisocial problems head-on. CNBC Make It spoke with 15 students, educators and mental health experts to see how we got here — and where we might be going.
Today’s college students were already at a disadvantage, socially speaking, well before stepping foot on campus.

Not only were they forced to isolate during middle school or high school because of the pandemic, many are also finding fewer spaces to meet in real life, as malls and movie theaters — traditional meeting grounds for young people — have shuttered in recent years. “A lot of them never had to build those muscles of how do you socialize in person,” says Chicago-based therapist Andrew Fishman.
For some teenagers, that inability to connect meant new norms. “I think a lot of people just got used to not hanging out with people after school,” says Harker about high school.

For others, it’s made approaching people that much scarier. The less you have a chance to talk to someone new, says Garrison, “the more anxious you are going to be about engaging in those types of activities.”

On campus, that could also mean high rates of loneliness. When asked how often they feel or felt lonely in college in a CNBC and SurveyMonkey poll conducted in August 2026, a quarter of 18-to 34-year-olds said “always” or “often,” versus just 14% of 35-to 64-year-olds. The modeled error estimate for this survey was plus or minus 3.0 percentage points.

When they finally reach the hallowed halls of their universities, many students are constantly connected to a device. Often, they are heads down in screens or engrossed in whatever’s happening in their headphones.

Before class, 19-year-old Karla Berrueto, a junior in standing at the University of Houston, reports: “No one really talks to each other.” Twenty-one-year-old Jean Antoine, a senior at Loyola Marymount University, offers a similar appraisal. At the dining hall, it’s “more of people with AirPods and watching YouTube sitting alone” than talking, he says.

Even when people go out of their way to connect offline, they’re frequently stymied. Franco Geldart, a 20-year-old sophomore at Northeastern University, joined a cooking club his freshman year. He found striking up conversations with people a bit awkward. Often, “I was sitting [there] for an hour and I didn’t speak with a single person,” he says.

Most of the students CNBC Make It spoke with attended up to a handful of parties per year. Some described them as events you attend with friends and leave, rather than fluid opportunities to engage with new people.

Asked how often they initiate or initiated conversations with people at school they didn’t know, 31% of Gen Z said “rarely” or “never,” according to the CNBC and SurveyMonkey poll, versus 26% of Millennials and 22% of Gen X.
Another new element of today’s campus is the plethora of online platforms on which one can be called out for doing … anything, really, making even the most mundane decisions terrifying.

Yik Yak and Fizz are anonymous digital message boards. Fizz alone is live at more than 800 U.S. college campuses, according to its website. Many schools also have dedicated Barstool Sports Instagram pages, often affiliated with the popular sports blog but unaffiliated with the schools. All three may contain posts making fun of individual students’ behavior.

Harker remembers going to a football game her freshman year and losing the friend she came with. She felt paralyzed, scared of trying to befriend people who’d reject her and even more terrified of getting photographed sitting at the game by herself.
“If I just sat there alone,” she says she thought, “would I get on the Barstool page?” What would the social repercussions of that be?
Yik Yak, Fizz and Barstool Sports did not respond to CNBC Make It’s request for comment.
To be clear, young people are still forging connections on campus. They are figuring it out. Some are even experiencing similar levels of social fluidity as prior generations.
And some see what’s been happening on campus and taking action.

Geldart is working on an application for a new club at Northeastern this year called Wildcard. It would partner with existing clubs and do one-off drop-ins in which members from each club would be randomly paired up for a project.
“It’s just to get people talking,” he says.

At New York University, students have spearheaded a campus-wide initiative called NYU IRL, centered on connecting in the age of technology. With the help of a coalition of deans, faculty, staff and grad students, NYU IRL projects include phone-free spaces, a phone breakup challenge with Catherine Price, author of “How to Break Up With Your Phone,” and a video series about how to make small talk. More than 1,000 students have signed up for the phone breakup challenge alone.

For her part, Harker found someone she knew at the football game where she’d lost her friend and the two became each other’s go-to game date. She joined a sorority and now lives in a house with a number of her friends.

Harker’s working on creating more opportunities for people to meet. She remembers attending one house party her freshman year, for example. “It was the best experience I ever had,” she says. It was an easy, casual way to get to know people. Harker and her roommates are now trying to replicate that experience.
“We have this thing,” she says, “we’re going to bring back house parties.”

	Before class, 19-year-old Karla Berrueto, a junior in standing at the University of Houston, reports: “No one really talks to each other.” Twenty-one-year-old Jean Antoine, a senior at Loyola Marymount University, offers a similar appraisal. At the dining hall, it’s “more of people with AirPods and watching YouTube sitting alone” than talking, he says.
	Even when people go out of their way to connect offline, they’re frequently stymied. Franco Geldart, a 20-year-old sophomore at Northeastern University, joined a cooking club his freshman year. He found striking up conversations with people a bit awkward. Often, “I was sitting [there] for an hour and I didn’t speak with a single person,” he says.
	Most of the students CNBC Make It spoke with attended up to a handful of parties per year. Some described them as events you attend with friends and leave, rather than fluid opportunities to engage with new people.
	Asked how often they initiate or initiated conversations with people at school they didn’t know, 31% of Gen Z said “rarely” or “never,” according to the CNBC and SurveyMonkey poll, versus 26% of Millennials and 22% of Gen X.
	Another new element of today’s campus is the plethora of online platforms on which one can be called out for doing … anything, really, making even the most mundane decisions terrifying.
	Yik Yak and Fizz are anonymous digital message boards. Fizz alone is live at more than 800 U.S. college campuses, according to its website. Many schools also have dedicated Barstool Sports Instagram pages, often affiliated with the popular sports blog but unaffiliated with the schools. All three may contain posts making fun of individual students’ behavior.
	Harker remembers going to a football game her freshman year and losing the friend she came with. She felt paralyzed, scared of trying to befriend people who’d reject her and even more terrified of getting photographed sitting at the game by herself.
	“If I just sat there alone,” she says she thought, “would I get on the Barstool page?” What would the social repercussions of that be?
	Yik Yak, Fizz and Barstool Sports did not respond to CNBC Make It’s request for comment.
	To be clear, young people are still forging connections on campus. They are figuring it out. Some are even experiencing similar levels of social fluidity as prior generations.
	And some see what’s been happening on campus and taking action.
	Geldart is working on an application for a new club at Northeastern this year called Wildcard. It would partner with existing clubs and do one-off drop-ins in which members from each club would be randomly paired up for a project.
	“It’s just to get people talking,” he says.
	At New York University, students have spearheaded a campus-wide initiative called NYU IRL, centered on connecting in the age of technology. With the help of a coalition of deans, faculty, staff and grad students, NYU IRL projects include phone-free spaces, a phone breakup challenge with Catherine Price, author of “How to Break Up With Your Phone,” and a video series about how to make small talk. More than 1,000 students have signed up for the phone breakup challenge alone.
	For her part, Harker found someone she knew at the football game where she’d lost her friend and the two became each other’s go-to game date. She joined a sorority and now lives in a house with a number of her friends.
	Harker’s working on creating more opportunities for people to meet. She remembers attending one house party her freshman year, for example. “It was the best experience I ever had,” she says. It was an easy, casual way to get to know people. Harker and her roommates are now trying to replicate that experience.
	“We have this thing,” she says, “we’re going to bring back house parties.”

title: The RealReal CEO started as its first employee—her No. 1 lesson over 15 years: Don't 'get too attached to being right'
author: Tom Huddleston Jr.
description: Rati Sahi Levesque went from The RealReal's first employee to CEO, a journey that taught her the importance of curiosity and a growth mindset.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Leadership, RealReal Inc, Personnel, Wells Fargo & Co, Make It, Make It - Success, Make it - Level Up, Make It - Leadership, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: Rati Sahi Levesque never wants to forget the “really hard” times she experienced while working at The RealReal, she says. After all, they taught her how to lead a company worth north of $1 billion.

Levesque, 45, started working at the luxury resale marketplace in 2011 as its first employee and remembers struggling to get old-school fashion houses to understand its online business model. Later, as The RealReal’s chief operating officer during the Covid-19 pandemic, she keenly felt the company’s loss of “hundreds of millions of dollars,” she says.

Now, she’s The RealReal’s CEO, credited with overseeing one of the retail industry’s more successful post-Covid turnaround stories. Since her appointment in October 2024, Levesque has helped add nearly $1 billion to The RealReal’s market value, which sits at nearly $1.3 billion as of Thursday afternoon. The company brought in more than $692 million in 2025 revenue, according to its annual report. In September, Levesque landed on the 2026 Time100 Next List of the “world’s most influential rising stars.”

The rise from founding employee to chief executive gave Levesque firsthand experience in many of the roles at her company, and empathy for the 3,000-plus employees who work those jobs, she says. The No. 1 lesson she learned from her 15 years at the company, she says: Never lose your “growth mindset,” stay open to reevaluating your preconceived notions and be willing to accept when your strategy isn’t working.

“One of the biggest lessons I’ve learned is not to get too attached to being right,” says Levesque, 45. “We’ve made plenty of decisions over the years that we thought were the right ones at the time, only to learn there was a better way. You have to be able to laugh at yourself, acknowledge what isn’t working and move forward.”
The RealReal’s post-Covid success revolves around an acknowledgment of being wrong, Levesque says.

Like many venture-backed startups, The RealReal’s leadership team spent much of its first decade focused on growth at all costs, absorbing annual losses to prioritize acquiring new customers. Levesque was part of the team behind that strategy. But when the pandemic sent sales plummeting, the company’s leaders realized the need to “pare back” from less profitable categories, like home goods and children’s apparel, that they had previously added in the name of growing revenue, then-CEO John Koryl told The New York Times in August 2023.

The RealReal’s pandemic lows pushed the company to experiment and grow in other ways too, Levesque says. At the time, The RealReal ran several large, expensive brick-and-mortar retail locations — including a 6,000-square-foot store in New York City and a 12,000-square-foot one in Los Angeles — meant to allow shoppers to interact with some luxury items and staff in person before making a purchase. Depressed consumer foot traffic pushed the company’s leadership into taking “big bets” on closing those large stores in favor of a more efficient and economical approach, says Levesque.
The RealReal now manages a larger number of smaller stores, aiming for efficiency over spectacle, the company told The Wall Street Journal in 2024.

Analysts have credited The RealReal’s recent growth to Levesque and Koryl’s strategy, which included other cost-cutting measures such as layoffs and the introduction of artificial intelligence-powered tools meant to help authenticate large numbers of luxury goods efficiently. The moves helped give The RealReal “one of the best turnarounds” in the retail industry, Wells Fargo senior analyst Ike Boruchow wrote in an October 2025 research note.

The pandemic, of course, gave plenty of business leaders reason to change strategic course. Realizing you’re wrong and reacting with humility isn’t always so easy to do in regular day-to-day life, Levesque says.

As CEO, she observes how employees respond to setbacks to get a sense of their growth mindset, she says: Do they try to dodge responsibility or spin a loss as a win? Do they take accountability and show a willingness to learn something that will make them more effective in the future?

Levesque also suggests practicing being wrong, so you’re familiar with the feeling of knowing when your original idea is still worth pursuing and when to change course. She got a lot of practice by working in a whole host of different environments during her first 15 years at The RealReal, she notes.
“You’re going to fail. Like, it’s going to happen,” she says. “You’re going to get things wrong. But taking accountability for it really helps.”
