title: Parents who have the strongest relationships with their kids ask these 5 'revealing' questions, says conversation expert
author: Vanessa Van Edwards
description: "Conversation" author and public speaking expert Vanessa Van Edwards shares five low-stakes questions that will reveal how your kids are really feeling.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Children, Parenting, Arts and entertainment, Personal finance, Lifestyle, Make It, How to Talk to People , Make It - Success, Make It - Raising Successful Kids, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: We’ve all had moments like these, as both parents and kids: “What did you get up to today?” “Nothing.” “How was school today?” “Fine.”

Of course, you care about your kid and want to know what’s really going on with them. But the problem with questions like these is that they can create an unintentional conversational burden for your child.

After a long day, the last thing they want is another thing to think through. They also might worry that if they answer with anything other than “I’m fine,” they’ll get a wave of concern from us. That’s why many kids dislike these questions or default to “fine” — even if they aren’t.

As a behavioral researcher with over a decade of experience studying human conversation and connectedness, I’ve found that the questions that can give you the clearest sense of your child’s emotional state sound like they’re about something else on the surface. But the answers tell you a lot about what’s going on underneath.

They also have no one “good” or “right” answer that your kid feels like they have to defend. In practice, they should feel like a low-stakes game. You can use these lighter-hearted queries as a ladder to get to heavier topics. Of course, make sure you talk to your child’s physician if you have any major concerns about their well-being.
Start with these five questions to help you get the answers you’re searching for — and build stronger ties with your kid.

This is a great prompt for kids who typically refuse to answer questions. Most of the feedback kids get comes from adults. This question is special because it gives children the chance to compliment themselves, and establish a sense of agency, positivity and pride.

If they name a concrete skill, encourage it. You can also ask a follow-up question like, “How did you figure that out?” or “Can you teach me?” But if they say something along the lines of “Nothing, I guess,” they might not give themselves enough credit or feel safe bragging to you. If they draw a blank, name one skill you’ve noticed in them.
A kid will tell you about themselves through a character. Be sure to ask why they chose that character. Their explanation is more important than your interpretation.

The words they use matter. If they say “funny,” “brave” or “loyal,” that tells you what they’re proud of. Phrases like “nobody sees him” or “she’s always left out” might reveal how they feel they’re being treated right now.

If they tell you a specific hero or lead, they likely see themselves as the driver of their own story. If they’re a sidekick, they might feel a need to downplay their own importance. If they say a villain, don’t be alarmed. Plenty of villains are characters who are often misunderstood and your kid might be telling you they feel the same way.

This question replaces the more easily dodged “Are you okay?” Kids also tend to love this question because it’s more of a game than an obvious probe into their mood — even though it is something of a disguised emotional check-in.

If they offer you a funny title, they are likely in a light-hearted mood. If they give you a bleak or flat title, make a note and then ask a follow-up later that day like, “Why was your movie title ‘The Longest Tuesday Ever?’”
With that information, you can open up the lines of communication to help them problem-solve and feel better.

If they answer “nothing” or “sleeping,” they might be uninspired or running on empty. Feel free to skip the pep talk and ask what’s been taking up their energy lately. Sometimes “sleeping” just means it’s been a really long week.
If they respond with something creative like painting, or social like hanging out with friends, that’s a good indication of what boosts their energy, rather than drains it.

When you know what fuels them, look for ways to consistently include it in their routine, like 20 minutes of play after homework or a Saturday craft night with a friend. Let them pick when it happens so they want to continue doing it.

There are many social interactions kids have that parents aren’t privy to, especially for school-age children. These questions are revealing because they show when kids’ guards go up and down, even when they don’t realize it. Your child might be surprised by their own response.

Try your best to not react to their answer. If you flinch at the person who stresses them out, your kid learns what it costs to tell you things. Give them the space to talk about why they feel this way.

Identifying the people and environments that drain them is a valuable skill for kids. They can’t always choose who is in their class or family, but they can choose where they devote their energy and who they want to spend their free time with. You can help model that as well.

Ask these questions in the car, at dinner or at bedtime. But make sure not to ask too many in a row, or it’ll turn into an interrogation. Take a turn answering them yourself. It demonstrates that you’re willing to be open about your feelings, too.
When you stay curious and ask the right questions, eventually your child might bring up the thing that happened before you even have to ask.

Vanessa Van Edwards is a speaker, researcher and the author of ”Conversation: How to Connect with Anyone & Make Every Interaction Count,” ”Captivate: The Science of Succeeding with People″ and ”Cues: Master the Secret Language of Charismatic Communication.” She is the founder of Science of People, where she leads workshops and courses on science-based soft skills to help people become better communicators.

title: 19-year-old started a 3D-printing side hustle in his parents’ basement—now his business brings in $808K a year
author: Megan Sauer, Valentina Duarte
description: Mike Satterlee learned how to use 3D printers as a high school freshman. Now age 19, he's growing his business CruiseCup instead of attending college.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Entrepreneurship, Video First, Amazon.com Inc, Shopify Inc, New York, Entrepreneurs, Make It, Make It - Success, Make It - Power Players, Make It - How I Made It, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: Just three months after graduating high school, Mike Satterlee didn’t expect his business, which 3D prints and sells “can coolers” — hard-shell insulated drink coozies — to receive hundreds of orders in a single day.

Yet there he was, in August 2025, doing math to figure out how long his 60 printers in a 3,000-square-foot warehouse in Clifton Park, New York, would take to fulfill the demand. The answer: about six weeks. The reason for all the demand: an Instagram post.

Satterlee had posted online about his company CruiseCup’s newest product, which could hold two 12-ounce cans at a time and reload from the top or the bottom, instead of having just one opening. After the “tactical reloader” went viral, Satterlee waited for enough revenue to buy more printers. CruiseCup brought in $100,000 that month, roughly 60% more than Satterlee had ever brought in monthly from his previous entrepreneurial endeavors, the 19-year-old says.

Unlike some viral businesses, CruiseCup built on that month’s momentum: It brought in $808,000 in 2025 gross revenue across its website and TikTok Shop, according to documents reviewed by CNBC Make It, and a marginal amount more from Amazon sales, says Satterlee.

3D-printing businesses are relatively easy to start and inexpensive to run. From October 2025 through September 2026, the number of 3D-printed products sold on Shopify increased 112%, according to a company spokesperson. Still, few founders share Satterlee’s combination of youth and ability to grow his business quickly. CruiseCup is profitable, but Satterlee only pockets some of the proceeds — $500 to $1,500 per month — because he lives with his parents and doesn’t pay rent, he says. The rest typically goes toward more 3D printers, social media ads or developing new products, he notes. (Satterlee declined to share CruiseCup’s specific annual profit figures.)

Satterlee runs the company full-time with one other employee, selling can coolers of varying sizes and materials. His previous businesses ranged from lemonade stands to selling homemade sand repellent lotion, a combination of hand sanitizer and cornstarch, he says. He learned how to use a 3D printer in a “design and drawing for production” class during his freshman year of high school, and used his savings from Christmas, birthdays and earlier ventures to buy a roughly $500 version for himself in September 2022, he says.

He launched his first 3D-printing business, which made and sold shoe charms designed to attach to Crocs, in his parents’ basement in June 2023. That business, called Solefully, brought in roughly $250,000 in 2024 sales, Satterlee estimates — enabling him in November 2024 to start renting the $3,600-per-month warehouse where he keeps his growing fleet of printers.

A few months before graduation, Satterlee decided that Solefully’s traction was promising enough to skip college and make it his full-time job, he says. He started experimenting with new products, and found that universal car cupholder adapters — which could hold any drink, from a Starbucks beverage to a Stanley water bottle — garnered more interest on social media and sold with higher profit margins than the shoe charms. CruiseCup eclipsed Solefully quickly enough for Satterlee to shut down the latter in June 2025.

The teenager designed the double-can coolers two months later, after scrolling on Instagram and seeing competing products that required the user to remove both cans to access their second drink, he says. He has two patents pending on CruiseCup designs, documents show.

Some of Satterlee’s high school classmates are now in their sophomore year of college. Satterlee says he’s committed to CruiseCup full-time, using 160 printers now to produce plastic products in New York and sourcing stainless steel models from a Chinese manufacturer that he found online. He plans to grow the business by adding UV printing — an alternative to screen printing — and more kinds of drinkware to its offerings. He wants to hire a larger marketing team to try getting CruiseCup onto retail shelves, he adds.
“Every day I wake up, I’m excited to go to work,” says Satterlee. “I don’t really even see it as work. I love what I do, I love building stuff and it makes it not even feel like work. It’s just fun.”

title: Dead mascots, neon labels and internet trends: Inside the strategy wars to capture Gen Z's spending power
author: Megan Sauer
description: Brands of all sizes are tailoring their marketing strategies to reel in Gen Z shoppers, sometimes going to extreme lengths to get their attention online.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Video First, United States, Sports, Arts and entertainment, Duolingo Inc, Target Corp, Tesla Inc, Make It, Make It - Success, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: When launching their company Good Girl Snacks in February 2024, Leah Marcus, 26, and Yasaman Bakhtiar, 27, knew they’d need a distinct look for their debut product, Hot Girl Pickles.

Pickle aisles, to them, all looked the same. Bland. Sanitized. Chartreuse. The founders instead aimed for a marketing hook and brand look “that were completely the opposite” of what conventional food brands do, says Marcus. They went with neon pink and turquoise labels, and Instagram posts of dill pickles wrapped in condoms and blunts.
The message wasn’t supposed to look delicious. It was a statement: “Everything we do is to create a reaction,” Marcus says.
Young customers, online and in stores like Erewhon, are here for it.

Gen Z consumers — those ages 14 to 29, specifically — tend to appreciate an unvarnished approach from brands, says Americus Reed, a marketing professor at The Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania. They engage with marketing that clearly shows what individual brands value — whether it’s style, the environment or a tastier, sexier pickle — so they can use the same branding to tell their friends and followers what matters to them, Reed says.

Brands that appeal to Gen Z act “less like a billboard and more like a box of identity Legos,” Reed says. The products they buy attempt to “help these Gen Zers communicate something, whether it be, ‘Hey, I am creative, I’m iconic, I’m environmentally aware, health conscious, rebellious, inclusive, culturally informed.’ Or, you know, just simply, ‘Hey, I’m in on this joke.’”

More companies are catching on. Some like Bakhtiar and Marcus opt for dynamic color palettes and spicy missives, while others create self-deprecating mascots and smart brand collaborations. Everyone seems to be participating in internet trends.

But making inroads with a customer who responds positively to condom-wearing pickles is easier said than done, and there certainly isn’t a one-size-fits-all strategy. The trick is acting fast when memes strike and doing it in a way that feels authentic to the brand, because Gen Zers “can tell when there’s an ingenuine-ness to it,” says 25-year-old Rand Rivera, who works for New York-based marketing agency, Athletics, and runs his own eponymous branding agency.

Few brands have mastered the approach better than Duolingo. The Pittsburgh-based language learning platform and its cartoon owl mascot, Duo, has amassed over 18 million followers on TikTok. The interest has been driven largely by the brand’s casual, sarcastic tone and active participation in online trends.

Duo has danced to viral music, dressed up like celebrities, and had tea with other characters from the Duolingo universe in an empty, yellow-wallpapered room, a reference to the internet trend that inspired the 2026 horror movie “Backrooms.” In one of Duolingo’s most viral online campaigns, Duo temporarily died after being hit by a vehicle resembling a Tesla Cybertruck.

The owl’s antics tell young users that Duolingo understands their sense of humor, says Rivera. The consistency of Duo’s voice over time matters too, he says, because many Gen Zers can catch inauthenticity and overt marketing from a mile away.

That consistent effort has been deliberate, says Katherine Chan, Duolingo’s director of brand marketing. “Gen Z is more media savvy, I think, than any generation that has come before, and is very aware of how much they’re being marketed to. And so you have to sort of jump into conversations that are already happening versus trying to make your own moment happen,” says Chan.
“Winking at that is sort of like a self-awareness that I think Gen Z really appreciates,” she adds.

Some Gen Z entrepreneurs have an advantage when trying to connect with their own demographic. Marcus and Bakhtiar, for example, say they intuitively know how to use tone to connect with an online audience.

“We’re a generation that really hates being advertised to in a very overt way,” says Bakhtiar, adding that brands today don’t even need to show their products in online posts anymore to get people’s attention. The co-founders might instead post pickle martini recipes, or keep the camera on themselves as they tell stories about the mishaps that come with starting and running a business together as friends in their 20s.

Their tone, reminiscent of FaceTime calls or “get ready with me” videos, helps Gen Z viewers feel like they’re getting cool recommendations from a friend, rather than witnessing a brand begging for their attention, Marcus and Bakhtiar say.
The strategy makes viewers feel like they actually know the co-founders, keeping them coming back for more — and building trust and brand loyalty over time, Marcus adds.

Colors, fonts and mascots may change with evolving trends, but the core of some traditional marketing strategies can still work on Gen Z: Shoppers, no matter their age, want to know how products can add value to their lives, says Kelly Pedersen, partner and global leader of retail at PwC. They want to know as directly and visually as possible, a lesson that peanut butter company One Trick Pony learned somewhat by accident, says co-founder and CEO Lucy Dana, 35.

When the Washington, D.C.-based brand launched in 2022, it packaged its natural peanut butter in a standard glass jar. After customers complained about the oil that floats to the top of natural peanut butter, the company created a plastic container that could sit upside-down on grocery store shelves, Dana says. The uniquely shaped pastel-colored jar offered more design real estate, so the company enlarged its explanatory language to the lids: “One more trick! Our specially-designed peanut butter jar helps reduce natural oil separation.”

“I’d say we took off because of these jars,” says Dana. Since the July 2025 redesign, which One Trick Pony announced on Instagram, the brand has tripled its social followers and landed placement on retail shelves in Target and other grocery stores across the U.S. Dana declined to share specific revenue figures but says the startup’s sales have quintupled so far in 2026 compared to 2025.

Still, some of Gen Z’s spending patterns are different than past generations, Pedersen notes: Instead of just caring about price or convenience, they want to use products to brand and market themselves to their own followers. They may prioritize buying from or posting about brands that are environmentally friendly, politically active or part of a larger cultural trend, like 2025′s Labubu craze. Their posts tell the people around them who they are, which means the products they prefer can play a key role in defining their identity among their friends, adds Reed, the Wharton marketing professor.

“Gen Z, I think they want the whole experience,” Pedersen says. “If they’re going to pay maybe $30 for a squishy toy or something, they want to [buy into] a whole squishy toy world,” ranging from raptly following the brand’s social media storytelling to hosting real-life events that bring other fans together.

For brands, finding fans among Gen Z may have an added benefit of shifting algorithms in their favor. Because Gen Zers are so online, they contribute to and partially dictate social media algorithms for consumers of every age, Pedersen says. In other words, the more they view, like and share a certain kind of content, the more likely it is to be distributed on other people’s social media feeds.

Gen Z’s spending power is increasingly influential, too. When compared with millennials at the same age, and adjusted for inflation, Gen Zers’ household income is 25% higher and their overall spending is 16% more, according to a PwC analysis of Bureau of Labor Statistics data.

“I think it’s an existential threat to be ignoring this demographic right now,” Pedersen says. “It’s not just about offering products that are geared toward younger people ... It’s bigger messaging. It’s a bigger campaign. It’s about engaging with that customer in a different way to bring them in and discover your brand.”

At Good Girl Snacks, early returns show signs of success. The co-founders declined to share revenue or profitability figures, but the company’s valuation reached $8.5 million after a $3 million seed fundraising round in March, as CNBC Make It reported on Aug. 29.
“The whole strategy has been to start niche, to know who our audience is,” Marcus says.

Strictly Necessary: These Cookies are required for Service functionality, including for system administration, delivering requested content and features, security and fraud prevention, to identify and fix technical issues, authenticate your identity, and to enable purchasing capabilities. These Cookies also allow your device to receive and send information, so you can see and interact with ads and content.
Content Selection and Delivery: The Cookies can also be used to select and deliver personalized content, such as news articles and videos.

Ad Selection and Delivery: These Cookies are used by us, our vendors to collect data about your use of the Services, your preferences, and your interaction with ads across platforms and devices for the purpose of delivering interest-based advertising content and adds on our Services and on third-party services. Typically, to opt out, such devices require you to select options like “limit ad tracking” or to disable options such as “interest-based advertising,” “interactive TV,” or “smart interactivity”. title: How much money buys happiness? Ray Dalio weighs in
author: Sawdah Bhaimiya
description: "Happiness past a certain level is not correlated with wealth," billionaire Ray Dalio said at the Milken Institute Asia Summit in Singapore on Thursday.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Ray Dalio, Lifestyle, Arts and entertainment, Make It - Success, Leadership, Make It - Money, Health Tips and Wellness Advice, Make It - Science of Success, Make It, Make It - Power Players, source:tagname:CNBC Europe Source
paragraphs: Self-made billionaire Ray Dalio has shared his wisdom on happiness and success, saying that wealth, in fact, does not determine your state of fulfilment.

The Bridgewater Associates founder has a net worth of nearly $22 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaire Index, and is among the 400 richest Americans. He and his wife, Barbara Dalio, have pledged to give away much of their wealth to philanthropic causes.

“Money’s an important consideration in terms of life, but really, if you even look at happiness, happiness past a certain level is not correlated with wealth,” the 77-year-old said on a panel at the Milken Institute Asia Summit in Singapore on Thursday. “The greatest determinant of happiness is a sense of community.”
Dalio added: “There’s a saying: ‘Success isn’t determined by how smart you are. It’s more determined by how adaptive you are.’”
Dalio founded Bridgewater in 1975, scaling it into one of the world’s largest hedge fund managers, which currently oversees about $102 billion for institutional clients.
He is also the author of the No. 1 New York Times bestseller “Principles,” which lays out his approach to decision-making and leadership.
Dalio emphasized at the Thursday summit that his mantra as a leader is balancing meaningful work with meaningful relationships
“We’re on a mission together, and then it becomes you need tough love,” he said. “You want tough love with your kids; you want tough love with everything because tough makes you stronger.”
He explained that to make a team successful, tough love is needed to hold them accountable.
The billionaire has similar views on achieving success.
Achieving success is about identifying your goals, mapping out a path, and then pursuing those goals with complete conviction, he said in a LinkedIn post in 2024.
“People who achieve success and drive progress deeply understand the cause-effect relationships that govern reality and have principles for using them to get what they want,” Dalio wrote at the time.

“I don’t care whether you want to be a master of the universe, a couch potato, or anything else—I really don’t. Some people want to change the world, and others want to operate in simple harmony with it and savor life. Neither is better. Each of us needs to decide what we value most and choose the paths we take to achieve it.”

title: The business of women's sports is booming—a viral bar that brings in $1M a year wants to take advantage
author: Tom Huddleston Jr.
description: As women's sports enjoy record viewership, The Sports Bra — a Portland, Oregon, bar that only plays women's sports on TV — is rolling out national franchise plans.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Entrepreneurship, Caitlin Clark, Sports, Reddit Inc, Nike Inc, Portland, OR, Entrepreneurs, Make It, Make It - Success, Make it - Level Up, Make It - Start-ups, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: As the 2026 WNBA Playoffs roar through its semifinal round, one thing is abundantly clear: Women’s sports are on fire.

Beyond record viewership totals, the business of women’s sports has been on a tear. Nike’s launch of Indiana Fever star Caitlin Clark’s first-ever signature sneaker — the Caitlin 1 — nearly sold out in less than two hours. Meanwhile, advertising spending on women’s sports has grown by 120% since 2022, Nielsen reports, and women’s sports are projected to generate roughly $3 billion in global revenue in 2026, triple that of two years ago, according to Deloitte.

Few entrepreneurs have taken advantage of the increased nationwide interest in women’s sports quite like Jenny Nguyen, the owner of The Sports Bra, a Portland, Oregon-based sports bar, which only plays women’s sports.

Nguyen, 46, put up her life savings — about $27,000 — to open her dream business in April 2022, CNBC Make It reported in April 2023. Despite its niche premise, the bar promptly brought in nearly $1 million in revenue and achieved profitability in its first eight months. It has brought in more than $1 million annually since then, Nguyen now says.

With the continuing rise of Americans’ interest in — and willingness to spend on — women’s sports, Nguyen decided to launch a crowdfunding effort on May 18 aimed at expanding The Sports Bra into a national franchise. Her goal was twofold. First: Open a larger location in Portland to accommodate more customers and host events for additional revenue. Second: Open up to roughly 40 franchise locations across the country, each modeled after the bigger Portland location, by 2030.

The campaign raised nearly $1.24 million from more than 1,400 people in roughly two months, reflecting the current financial heft of women’s sports and its fans: Nearly half of new investors on Republic, the platform Nguyen used, chose to give the campaign’s minimum investment of $250.
“The ability for the general public to buy into what we’re doing and be a part of the women’s sports movement is really, really exciting,” says Nguyen.

Amid the excitement, Nguyen is navigating a tightrope. She’s trying to grow The Sports Bra quickly enough to successfully leverage its popularity — without overextending her still-budding business, which could risk the brand she’s put everything into building.
Initially, Nguyen wasn’t sure her idea of a bar playing only women’s sports would work at all.

The lifelong basketball fan and trained chef was inspired by what she now calls a “pretty universal” experience: struggling to find a women’s sporting event, in her case the 2018 NCAA women’s basketball championship game, on the televisions at sports bars. She came up with The Sports Bra’s name years before actually attempting to launch the business, she told CNBC Make It in April 2023.
“It was catchy. I thought it was hilarious,” said Nguyen.

Social justice movements during the Covid-19 pandemic, most notably the #MeToo movement and protests following the murder of George Floyd, led her to take her idea more seriously, she said. The Sports Bra, she reasoned at the time, could be a place where people like herself — who had felt excluded from traditional sports establishments — would feel like they belonged.
“Me, personally, I thought the idea was brilliant and that [it was] what the world needs,” Nguyen said. “But I had no idea that the world would want it. I just wanted to give it a shot.”

While The Sports Bra was initially an outlier, much has changed since. Front Office Sports, a sports business news website, pegged the number of women’s sports-focused bars in the U.S. at 27, noting that the total quadrupled in 2025 alone.

The growing number of bars for women’s sports comes against the backdrop of a decrease in American discretionary spending. In 2025, 37% of Americans reported eating out less often, according to market researcher YouGov’s 2025 U.S. Dining Out Report, while bars especially have seen alcohol sales stagnate as a result of more Americans cutting back on drinking.

In a sense, sports bars are particularly vulnerable, as they typically need to pay for commercial licensing fees — required to display major sporting events, they can range from $1,100 to more than $300,000 annually depending on the establishment’s legal occupancy limit — that many other bars don’t need to pay.

The Sports Bra itself isn’t immune. Its revenue dipped 18% year-over-year to $1.02 million in 2025, according to a financial disclosure filed to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Aug. 6. And Nguyen’s establishment hasn’t had a profitable year since 2024, when in April it announced its franchising plans as part of an investment partnership with Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian’s 776 Foundation.

Nguyen now says that steadily increasing merchandise sales and an ever-growing roster of high-profile business partners, from the WNBA to Nike, make her confident in the staying power of her brand. Plus, she’s been reinvesting in the business, as the company builds out a team to oversee franchising and expansion, says Nguyen. Traditionally, that investment starts to pay off once new locations open and start producing revenue of their own. The Sports Bra has lined up franchisees in five cities so far — Boston, Las Vegas, Indianapolis, St. Louis and Portland, Maine — with plans for the St. Louis location to open by the end of October.

Nguyen projects generating $75 million in annual revenue across 40 locations in four years. She’s quick to point out that’s a best-case scenario, calling it a “moonshot” figure based on the $25,000 in annual revenue that the original Portland location brings in per seat. That location seats up to 40 people, whereas the larger venues in Portland and across the country will hold more than twice as many customers, she says.
To hit her revenue goal within four years, Nguyen understands that a lot has to go right, starting with the rollout of the first five franchise locations.
“Everybody’s watching, and if [the first five] don’t launch well, then we can kind of kiss the 40 [locations] in four years goodbye,” she says.

Interest from sports fans helped turn The Sports Bra into something of a national brand, attracting a range of visitors and investors ranging from Ohanian to Renee Montgomery, a former WNBA player who is co-owner of the league’s Atlanta Dream. It also opened the door for increased competition, one of the many obstacles that Nguyen acknowledges could derail her ambitious growth plans.

The Sports Bra’s first five franchise locations have all experienced delays in opening, Nguyen says, from permitting issues to procuring kitchen equipment and extended construction timelines. Those delays mean a longer wait for additional revenue streams to turn on, as business costs for small businesses nationwide increase due to inflation, tariffs and ongoing global conflicts.

Franchising often comes with other pitfalls, too — especially when done rapidly, and at great scale. A standalone business’ popularity can be difficult to recreate in multiple new locations, especially if the parent company doesn’t have enough infrastructure or trained staff to maintain consistency and quality. With enough shuttered franchises or damage to the overall brand, premature franchise scaling can bring down an entire business.

For The Sports Bra especially, an immediate franchise flop from an industry standard-bearer could do more than just derail Nguyen’s expansion plans. It could raise questions about the broader viability nationwide of business models revolving only around women’s sports and their fans.

“It’s critical that we nail it,” says Nguyen, adding that successful franchising often stems from the franchisee selection process. “When we choose our franchise owners ... it is based on their love of our mission, values, and purpose of the Bra. If that’s not there, this is not going to work out.”

Her expansion goal is so audacious — 40 locations in four years — partially because she doesn’t want to be too passive and let this moment of opportunity slip away, she says. And while she’s broadly supportive of growing community around businesses that support women’s sports, she’s competitive enough to want The Sports Bra to step into any new market and quickly differentiate itself enough to become the dominant player, she says.
In short, she wants to win.

“I will never take it lightly that we were, kind of, first to market, and that folks continue to look up to The Sports Bra,” Nguyen says. “How do we continue to set the bar really high, and then have [competitors] level it up, and then us try to do the same, back and forth, back and forth? I’m wicked into that.”

title: Nonprofit received $2 million from Olivia Rodrigo and Melinda French Gates—it wants to give cash to abuse survivors
author: Megan Sauer
description: The money nonprofit Freefrom received from participating in Olivia Rodrigo's Daisy Chain Music Festival helped the organization hit its annual finacial goal.
keywords: makeit, Articles, ETSY Inc, Make It, Make It - Success, Make It - Start-ups, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: At 4 p.m. on Saturday, August 29, leaders from the 10 nonprofits involved in Olivia Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields music festival stood, arms linked, huddled in the corner of a hangar. The group, who spent the day running booths inside the facility to introduce festival goers to their work, was told to meet for an announcement, but given no other context, says FreeFrom founder and CEO Sonya Passi.

Standing shoulder to shoulder, they leaned in so they could hear the news above the noise of the fans inside the hangar. Melinda French Gates was matching the $10 million proceeds raised by the event, a member of Rodrigo’s team told them. That meant that FreeFrom and the other nonprofits — which included Planned Parenthood, Baby2Baby and Black Mamas Matter Alliance — would each take home $2 million, twice the amount previously announced at a press conference the day before the festival.

“We were all crying,” Passi, 38, says, adding: “As a founder and CEO, you’re always balancing your time between raising money to do the work and doing the work. Getting that $2 million allows me to put more of my attention right now into doing the work ... and to think further ahead about building strategies that are more long-term and ultimately more effective.”

FreeFrom is a nonprofit working to end gender-based violence through economic interventions. The organization gives money — by way of career-building grants, a savings matching program and an emergency cash program — to survivors of abuse and advocates for statewide and federal policies that support survivors’ financial security. The $2 million donation will go toward current and future initiatives, like its cash-based programs and their survivor collective, which has 600 members, Passi says.

“This $2 million means that we have raised the amount of money we needed this year to break even,” Passi says. Since its founding in 2016, FreeFrom has always ended each calendar year in the black, she notes, while adding: “I’ve had years where that moment doesn’t come until the end of the year.” That’s the norm for many nonprofits, which often rely on donations to keep their organizations alive. Nonprofits received 37% of all 2025 online revenue in December, according to nonprofit database M+R Benchmarks’ annual report including 180 nonprofits.

Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields Music Festival — which donated all its proceeds to nonprofits and included performances from musicians like Chappell Roan and Doechii — was modeled after Lilith Fair, a traveling music festival co-founded by singer Sarah McLachlan in 1997 that featured only female artists. Rodrigo was inspired to launch her own festival after watching girls and women connect in the crowd at her concerts, she told Rolling Stone on September 3. “I’ve always been so acutely aware of the power of [coming together],” she said. “And also I’ve always been really passionate about women’s rights and reproduction healthcare, and so it just felt like a perfect thing to do.”

Some data shows Gen Z — Rodrigo is 23 — are likelier to participate in philanthropic causes than older generations. Over 70% of Gen Z Americans reported they “gave in some form,” through donations, volunteering, fundraising or advocacy work, within the previous week, according to a 2026 survey with over 10,000 respondents conducted by GivingTuesday and GoFundMe between January 2025 and January 2026. That compares with roughly 65% of older adults who said they gave during the week prior.

Passi, who became an activist at 16, founded FreeFrom a decade ago after realizing how big a role money played in survivor’s independence. Three quarters of women who called the National Domestic Violence Hotline reported staying longer with a controlling partner because they were concerned about supporting themselves or children, according to survey data from over 1,800 women analyzed by Michigan State University researchers. Survivors need an average of $1,567 “to make ends meet and stay safe,” but only have an average of $10 in savings and less than $300 that they can access alone, according to FreeFrom research.
Passi says she was in complete shock when she heard from Rodrigo’s team, who reached out to FreeFrom in June and asked if Passi would be willing to hop on a Zoom call with Rodrigo herself.
“We’re so lucky … I don’t know how they found us, but I’m grateful they did,” Passi says.

At the festival, FreeFrom’s booth was located in the northeast corner of the event’s grounds, past a Yoko Ono-inspired wish tree and Etsy-sponsored fountain of jewelry beads. Passi and the other nonprofit representatives walked over to one of the stages at 8 p.m. to hear Rodrigo and French Gates announce the updated $20 million donation to the crowd, then spent the evening listening to music, she says. Rodrigo performed with guests like McLachlan, Alanis Morissette and Stevie Nicks. Ten giant, vintage-looking buttons, each representing a nonprofit in attendance, were seemingly fastened to the top of the stage.

“What I heard from Olivia and her team over again was they wanted people to feel joy, and that’s so in line with what FreeFrom aims to do,” Passi says. “We want to change the conversation around gender-based violence to focus on ... possibility and survivors’ joy, because I know that is how you build a movement.”

title: Automation will affect 36 million jobs by 2035—these 10 occupations could be hit hardest, says new report
author: Sophie Caldwell
description: Automation could affect 36 million jobs by 2035, according to a recent report from the McKinsey Global Institute.
keywords: makeit, Articles, United States, Personnel, Labor economy, Social issues, Make It, Make It - Work, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: Approximately 7 percent of the U.S. workforce — 11 million employees — may need to switch occupations within the next decade, according to a report from McKinsey Global Institute published on Sept. 29.

Boosted by the AI boom, the U.S. economy could create over 40 million new jobs in the next decade, the report found, but widespread adoption of AI and other automation technologies could also reduce demand for existing jobs by 21%, equivalent to 36 million jobs’ worth of labor, by 2035.
Roughly 25 million workers will be able to stay in their current occupations, although the nature of their jobs may change, while the remaining 11 million will need to pivot into other fields.
“The good news is that the demand is going to be higher than the decline,” says Tanguy Catlin, director of the McKinsey Global Institute.

But for workers whose jobs are affected by automation adoption, which the report defines as “the share of current work hours potentially automated or meaningfully augmented” by technology, the path ahead could be complicated, Catlin says.

According to the report, these are the top 10 jobs that will be most affected by automation adoption, based on the number of full-time employees, the estimated percentage of current work hours that will be affected, and the estimated reduction in labor demand due to automation.
1. Office and administrative support
Number of full-time employees: 18 million
Percentage of work hours affected: 81%
Reduced labor demand due to automation: 38%
2. Agriculture, fishing and forestry
Number of full-time employees: 400,000
Percentage of work hours affected: 76%
Reduced labor demand due to automation: 43%
3. Technology and analytics
Number of full-time employees: 5.2 million

According to Catlin, higher levels of automation adoption don’t always translate to less demand for workers. Some jobs are more likely to be “reinvented” or augmented by AI adoption, rather than replaced, he says.
For example, automation could affect 47% of work hours in the legal field, but the projected loss of labor demand is only 18%.
Lawyers “historically used to spend a lot of time doing research,” Catlin says, but today, AI can perform a lot of that research, so lawyers will spend more time on tasks that require human judgment.
“Your job role or title doesn’t change, but how you spend your time is changing massively,” he says.

With this data, Catlin says that it’s important to note that there is a difference between how much work is “theoretically automatable” versus “what is actually going to be automated” within organizations: according to the report, “Technology determines what is possible, but managerial choices determine how quickly those possibilities become reality.”
As such, the number of workers who will need to switch occupations could range between 6 and 16 million, with 11 million as the base estimate.
For the 11 million displaced workers, migrating into entirely new jobs “will not necessarily be easy,” Catlin says.

One in seven will have a “direct” pathway into new jobs in expanding fields, meaning that they can find roles that involve similar skills, require easy-to-acquire credentials and offer equal or better pay than their previous job.

But almost 45% could face an “unpaved” pathway, which means that finding a new job could require them to move geographically, significantly reskill or acquire new credentials — often for lower pay than their original roles.
“To get those credentials may require an investment of time and an investment of money, and that will be source of friction” for workers, Catlin says.

Moreover, for 11 million workers to land in new roles within the next decade, about 770,000 workers would need to switch occupational groups each year, a rate of change that is roughly 3.6 times the historical average.

It’s “feasible” for this transition to happen, Catlin says, but navigating it successfully will require a “system-level response” in which employers and the government invest in helping workers re-skill. Employees aren’t “able to address those gaps on their own,” he says.
In the meantime, Catlin advises workers to focus on developing skills like problem-solving, interpersonal communication, collaboration, critical thinking, curiosity and willingness to learn.
Those skills will “allow you to get access to better jobs” and “allow you to have resilience as the world continues to change,” he says.
“The pace of change will never be as slow as today,” he continues. “Therefore, we need to have a workforce that embraces adaptability, continuous improvement and continuous learning.”

title: Gen Zers quit their jobs to start a pickle company—now it’s valued at $8.5 million
author: Megan Sauer
description: Good Girl Snacks founders Leah Marcus and Yasaman Bakhtiar built their startup's multimillion-dollar valuation with pickle jars and Gen Z branding strategies.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Generation Z, Entrepreneurship, Brands and branding, Conagra Brands Inc, Kraft Heinz Co, Shopify Inc, Entrepreneurs, Make It, Make It - Success, Make It - Start-ups, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: At 4 a.m. on Monday, June 1, Leah Marcus woke up to 70 missed calls from her co-founder.

The good news: A prominent influencer, Alix Earle, had posted a TikTok video about Hot Girl Pickles, the debut product sold by Marcus and co-founder Yasaman Bakhtiar’s Los Angeles-based startup Good Girl Snacks. The bad news: Most of the video involved Earle struggling to open the pickle jar. “Imagine our horror,” said Marcus, partially joking, in a response video hours later. Next came adrenaline, when hundreds of orders flooded the startup’s Shopify store the following day, Marcus and Bakhtiar say.

Turning chaos into content is part of the recipe at Good Girl Snacks, which sells jars of Hot Girl Pickles nationwide online and in grocery stores including Whole Foods Market and Erewhon, and grab-and-go packets on its website and in smaller grocery stores. The startup declined to share revenue figures or profitability status, but was most recently valued at $8.5 million following a $3 million seed fundraising round in March, according to documents reviewed by CNBC Make It.

The co-founders tout original recipes, but at a fundamental level, they didn’t invent a new method to soak cucumbers in vinegar. Instead, Marcus, 26, and Bakhtiar, 27, say they’ve grown their startup around an aptitude for branding toward a Gen Z audience, both online and offline.

Each Hot Girl Pickles product has brightly colored pink, purple or teal packaging that visually stands out against the sea of legacy brands’ primary colors on grocery store condiment shelves. The co-founders’ tone drips with dryness, self-deprecation and a hint of sarcasm, when addressing their social media followers, including nearly 175,000 of them on Instagram — more than most traditional pickle brands, which generally aren’t as active online.
“Everything we do is to create a reaction,” says Marcus.

A business that’s online and atypical for its category is a positive for many Gen Zers, says Americus Reed, a marketing professor at The Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania. Currently aged 14 to 29, Gen Zers are in a life stage where building “social credibility” among their peers matters, Reed says. Posting online about niche products can help them express part of their identity to their followers, Reed says — like how a colorful jar of organic pickles may show that someone is a conscientious snacker, for example.

Pickles are an actual trend right now, too: 20-somethings pushed retail sectors into “peak pickle” this summer, says Marni Shapiro, co-founder research and consulting firm The Retail Tracker. Pickle-flavored snacks brought in $518 million in sales between February 2025 and February 2026, up nearly 40% from a similar time period the year prior, according to data from market research firm Circana cited by food giant Conagra in a May 18 news release.

Bakhtiar and Marcus, college friends who graduated from the University of Southern California in 2022, started out as two of those 20-somethings, sending each other TikTok videos about pickles every day as early as 2023, they say. They decided to quit their jobs and start their company together that summer, as trends like Hot Girl Walk and Girl Dinner hit a fever pitch on social media, inspiring their startup’s name and branding.
“Our brand doesn’t take itself seriously. We’re self-deprecating on social media all the time. We do things that aren’t typically done in our category,” says Marcus.

The pair solicited startup advice from their USC classmates Troy Bonde and Winston Alfieri — co-founders of pasta sauce startup Sauz — and industry experts on LinkedIn to learn about funding, operations and logistics, they say. They raised an undisclosed amount of money from friends and family, and Good Girl Snacks sold its first pickles direct-to-consumer through its website in February 2024, they say. All along, they posted on social media about the process of building their business and gained 24,000 Instagram followers by Day 1 of sales.

The following month, Marcus and Bakhtiar made another strategic decision based on their network’s advice, submitting applications to sell pickles at Erewhon and Whole Foods despite barely having any history as a business. Both applications were approved in 2025, widening Hot Girl Pickles’ audience to include less-online buyers.

Of course, Gen Z only makes up about 20% of the U.S. consumer market. As far as pickles go, the industry is still dominated by decades-old legacy brands like Mt. Olive and Vlasic, according to an August 2025 report from grocery delivery service Instacart. Mt. Olive sells 230 million jars of pickles, peppers and relishes per year, according to its website. Vlasic is owned by Conagra, which has a market cap of $7.72 billion, as of Friday’s market close.

Bakhtiar and Marcus say they plan to sell additional snacks beyond pickles, using a similar branding and marketing playbook to grow their customer base across other categories. They may face challenges they don’t expect: Their first-ever inventory order of pickles, for example, got accidentally frozen in shipping, resulting in 3,000 pounds of defrosted, soggy, crunch-less cucumbers, the co-founders say. Another early shipment got delayed by a crop-destroying storm in Mexico, they add.
The co-founders documented both episodes in an online series they dubbed “cucumber gate.” Such growing pains are opportunities for great social media content, they say.

title: 27-year-old locksmith spent $7,000 on tools, works around the clock in NYC: 'I'd never held a screwdriver in my life' before starting
author: Megan Sauer
description: Yona Sahar, founder of Locksmith Girl of NYC, spent two years learning the trade. Now, she runs her own business while working around the clock.
keywords: makeit, Articles, New York, New York City, Personnel, Make It, Make It - Success, Make It - Start-ups, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: Every night, 27-year-old Sahar Yona sleeps next to two phones and a laptop with the volume turned all the way up, so she can hear potential clients call at any time, she says.

Yona is a residential and commercial locksmith based in New York City who’s available 24 hours a day because as a self-employed business owner, “every job counts,” she says. She wants to earn as much money and build her clientele at Locksmith Girl of NYC, which she launched under its current name in July 2025, as quickly as she can, she says.

She has momentum on her side. In January, when business was slow, a video she posted on TikTok — where she told women in New York to call her if they felt unsafe asking men locksmiths to pick their locks at night — amassed over 600,000 views. Since then, she’s landed more jobs than ever, from men and women, up to 60 per week, she says. On her busiest day so far this summer, she worked from 4 a.m. to 1 a.m. the next morning, she says.

Yona isn’t an online influencer. Her account only has nine videos, as of Friday afternoon. But her message clearly resonated: Yona declined to share her personal income, noting that she charges varying rates based on the difficulty of each job, but says she now earns more money as a business owner than she previously did as a subcontractor working for larger locksmithing companies. The average annual salary for a locksmith in New York is $76,745, according to job site Indeed.

Yona, as a female locksmith, isn’t alone. Women make up less than 1% of the country’s over 5 million installation, maintenance and repair workers, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. However, more women than ever before are becoming locksmiths, according to anecdotal information provided by a spokesperson for the locksmith trade organization ALOA Security Professionals Association.

Locksmithing can feel tailor-made profession for “mechanically inclined” women who want to own their own business, says Jennifer Richards, a fourth-generation locksmith who’s run her family’s business in Hickory, North Carolina, for the last 31 years. Her six employees, including her sister-and-law and niece, are all related to her.

“Female locksmiths can think through problems and have a gentle touch,” says Richards, an ALOA member and instructor who notes that more women have taken her classes over the last three years. “Being light-handed is actually a benefit ... you can feel the movement [of the pins within the lock] a lot easier.”

A majority of locksmiths work solo, Richards estimates. While the equipment — like locks, drills and key-cutting machines — is costly, it’s a relatively attainable blue-collar business to start, considering you often only need a van, rather than a storefront and a team of employees, she says.

Yona spent $7,000 to buy her starting set of tools, she says. She got into the industry somewhat by happenstance: In 2021, she landed an interview for a receptionist position in a locksmith office. Her interviewer suggested that she had the temperament to work in the field, and that she should get her locksmith license, Yona says.

“I’d never held a screwdriver in my life,” she says. But she has a strong “go-getter” personality, and decided that being a female locksmith could give her a leg up in the male-dominated industry, she says. She spent two years training, applying for her license and buying her tools, she says. Then, she worked for subcontractors around the city to gain experience.

As a subcontractor, her work hours and income were relatively consistent and predictable throughout the year, she says. But all her co-workers were men, and she experienced misogyny from customers, peers and bosses, she says.

She decided to become her own boss in November 2024. The people who find Yona on TikTok know she works alone and are generally more patient, she says. Generally, she abides by the same strict boundaries with clients that she learned as a subcontractor, she says: She needs to see a photo or video of the lock and speak with the person on the phone before she accepts a job.

Still, she feels guilty when she takes an hour to relax in a bathhouse, play pool in a local bar or walk her dog, a German Shepherd-Rottweiler mix, in Central Park, she says. “The fear is that I can’t go too far from my car. My car is my legs,” she says, adding: “I’m supposed to be available.”

If Yona gets a call while out to dinner with a friend, the friend will often hop in Yona’s car and go with her to the job, she says. Those moments are becoming rarer, she says. She’s always thinking, and feeling a little paranoid, about work, and has begun scoping out a physical storefront for the Locksmith Girl of NYC in her downtime, she adds.
In other moments of free time, Yona practices picking locks. “I like the defiance” of the job, she says, legally getting into places intended to keep people out.

title: Gen Zers are making thousands of dollars a month running snail-mail subscription clubs: I don't think about expenses 'paycheck to paycheck anymore'
author: Megan Sauer
description: Some Gen Zers send art, letters, mini cookbooks and other forms of snail mail to paying subscribers — and make thousands of dollars per month in the process.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Entrepreneurship, Side Hustle, Entertainment, Entrepreneurs, Make It, Make It - Success, Make It - Start-ups, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: Kiki Klassen has a monthly routine: She spends hours neatly tucking typed letters and a 4 inch-by-6 inch printed postcard of one of her illustrations — both centered on an artistic theme, like “Year of the Horse” or “stars align” — into brightly-colored envelopes.

She repeats the process almost 900 times, one for each of her monthly subscribers, sometimes for six hours per night for an entire week at her dining room table in Niagara, Ontario. When finished, she heads to the post office. “I know all the ladies there by name, and they know me,” says Klassen, 28. “Sometimes they even help me put stamps on.”

Each subscriber to Klassen’s “snail-mail club,” called The Lucky Duck Mail Club — which she’s run as a side hustle since 2024 — pays roughly $8 per issue, and Klassen brings in a monthly average of roughly $4,385 in U.S. dollars in revenue, she says. She’s among a cohort of Gen Zers who’ve launched subscription-based mail services, where they send personal letters, art or zines to thousands of subscribers per month. Some ship out stickers and prints. Others specialize in jewelry and short stories.

Planning, creating and shipping the content can take weeks of work, but some make thousands of dollars in monthly profits, a variety of mail-club founders say. Most of the clubs gain traction on social media, with over 150,000 posts tagged with “Snail Mail” on TikTok.
DON’T MISS: The communication skill that can help you accelerate your career growth

In a way, the mail clubs are analog versions of Substack newsletters, and an example of Gen Z’s tendency to use the internet to popularize offline activities — like junk journaling, needlepointing or collecting CDs. Young professionals started spending more money on such tactile and nostalgic experiences during the Covid-19 pandemic, and continue to do so in the age of artificial intelligence, says Marni Shapiro, a co-founder and managing partner of research and consulting firm The Retail Tracker.

Klassen, a full-time social media manager at a restaurant group, has over 10,000 followers on TikTok and Instagram, respectively. Her biggest expense is paying for Canadian and American stamps — shipping 900 letters costs $2,000, she says — and her only paid employee is her sister-in-law. She maintains a roughly 70% profit margin, she says.
The mail club has “definitely created a cushiony security I didn’t have before,” says Klassen. “It’s been nice not to think about [expenses] paycheck to paycheck anymore.”

Other mail-club founders agree that having a social media following can help reel in subscribers quickly. Trinity Shiroma, an Orlando-based full-time artist, has over 49,000 followers on Instagram. Each month, she picks a landmark — like New York’s Metropolitan Museum, Paris’s Café De Flore or San Francisco’s The Painted Ladies — and paints it in detail on a 4-inch by 6-inch piece of paper.

Over two weeks, Shiroma paints the landmark and gets copies from a local print shop, writes an accompanying letter, and constructs a do-it-yourself craft. She spends another week packing everything into envelopes for her 2,700-plus subscribers, she says. She sells the original artwork on her website alongside other pieces of art, stickers and bookmarks.

The 25-year-old, who has a master’s degree in architecture from California Baptist University, sent her first round of snail mail in September, and had over 1,300 subscribers by December, she says. Shiroma’s service, called The Architecture Club, is the most lucrative part of her business, she adds: Each mailer costs roughly $2 and subscribers pay $8.88 per month. She made nearly $18,300 in profit for her May issue, she estimates.

“It’s not like I knew it was going to be a reliable source of income,” says Shiroma. “But I had already done the calculations. Even if I had one person subscribe, I’m still making, like, a $6-and-something profit.” Her mail club helped her and her husband save up to move into a larger apartment with four bedrooms, enough space for an office, a guest bedroom and her own personal studio, she says.
Klassen and Shiroma started their mail clubs after seeing other people boast online about the business model’s profitability, they say.

Bo Natakhin, a 26-year-old former fashion photographer, was similarly inspired, he says — to the point of making his cooking-themed mail club, called Little Kitchen of Bo, his full-time job before sending out a single issue. He put his first mini cookbook in the mail in late April, and almost 4,000 paying subscribers have received, or will soon receive, the 52-page zine containing pasta-related recipes.

Natakhin, who is based in Toronto, built his pre-launch follower base on TikTok, where he posted previews of the mini cookbook and footage of himself batching recipes in his kitchen. Each issue of Little Kitchen of Bo costs $20, and Natakhin plans to send a new one monthly, he says.

“I don’t think I have an apartment anymore. It’s more like a warehouse or studio,” says Natakhin. He worked up to 12 hour per day including weekends for a month to produce the first issue, he adds: Production equipment and boxes of printed zines replaced his living room couch, which is “now just sideways in our corridor.”

Before March, when Natakhin decided to commit to a mail club full-time, he earned income mostly through photography and gig work, he says. If Little Kitchen of Bo proves profitable enough, he hopes to move with his wife to Paris and enroll in Le Cordon Bleu cooking school, he notes. Building up the requisite savings could take some time, since the mail club also helps pay their household expenses, he says.

Beyond the potential earnings, running a mail club can give some founders extra business experience or career confidence. The success of Klassen’s side hustle emboldened her to seek a promotion at work in May 2025, she says: Then a barista, she pitched herself directly to the restaurant group’s owner for the social media role she now holds.
“I definitely got brave because of how Lucky Duck was going and making money ... and I think being a little bit brave and audacious got their attention,” Klassen says.

title: These Americans are quitting before AI can take their jobs—and starting their own businesses: 'I just wanted to be in control'
author: Megan Sauer, Sarah Jackson, Sophie Caldwell
description: Americans are incorporating new businesses in record numbers, as AI sweeps across many U.S. workplaces. That's not a coincidence, some new entrepreneurs say.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Entrepreneurship, Personnel, United States, Block Inc, Amazon.com Inc, Salesforce Inc, Intuit Inc, Toast Inc, Entrepreneurs, Make It, Make It - Success, Make It - Start-ups, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: Travis Di Lombardi-Spicer quit his audio producing job on the spot after getting passed up for a raise in January 2025. The 30-year-old felt artificial intelligence could eventually eliminate his job, and he wanted to do something proactive instead of pocketing his roughly $75,000 a year, from full-time work and freelance projects, and waiting for the end to come, he says.

Skeptical he’d find stability in an uncertain job market, Spicer turned to entrepreneurship. He spent $40,000 — selling some personal assets and pulling money from his 401(k) and savings — to launch the beta version of Spotbookr, his AI-powered consumer spending and advertising analytics business, in May 2025, he says.

Entrepreneurs in the U.S. filed 1.56 million business applications from November through January, the most of any three-month period since at least 2004, according to a CNBC Make It analysis of U.S. Census Bureau data. To an extent, the rise is predictable — when people struggle to find jobs, particularly against the backdrop of a stagnant job market or mass layoffs, they’re more likely to start businesses.

This crop of entrepreneurs is different: Anticipating future layoffs, some Americans are leaving their jobs preemptively to start businesses. Many of them say AI makes launching a startup easier. Others say they’re leaving on their own terms before suffering AI-related job cuts. Spicer became an example of both after experimenting with the technology himself, he says.
“Budgets [for audio projects] started getting lower and lower and lower,” says Spicer. “I just wanted to be in control.”
DON’T MISS: The leadership skills that can help you stand out at work

Entrepreneurship is notoriously risky. Roughly a quarter of new U.S. businesses don’t survive their first year, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data. But workers are also wary of the risks threatening typical 9-to-5 roles, with future-of-work reports and big-name CEOs predicting widespread workforce changes.

In a Resume Now poll from December of 1,012 employed U.S. adults, four in 10 workers said AI was already “replacing, devaluating, or overlapping” with elements of their job, and 29% said it could effectively do at least half of their daily responsibilities.

When you add geopolitical instability, rising costs of living and an erosion of trust between employers and employees, working Americans face a perfect storm of unpredictability, says Saikat Chaudhuri, faculty director of the entrepreneurship hub at the University of California, Berkeley’s Haas School of Business. The result is a record number of Americans seeking greater control over their careers, income and time, he says.
“The opportunity cost [of starting a business] is lower right now, just because the alternatives in the labor market are not as strong,” says Chaudhuri.

Five years into Michelle Yeung’s software engineering career at a large national media outlet, she felt unfulfilled and unhappy, she says. She made enough money — $250,000 per year, including bonuses — but the more advanced AI became, the more she could see it eventually replacing her, she says. She felt purposeless, she adds.

“I wasn’t really pushing myself. I wasn’t satisfied with how much I was growing or doing,” says Yeung, 29. Other factors beyond AI played into her job dissatisfaction, she notes. Still, “I wanted to go from giving, like, 20% of myself to giving 200% to something,” she says.

Yeung left her job in early 2025 and used her savings to open Matcha House, a cafe in New York’s East Village, that July, she says. “I just love physically being able to make something and then hand it to someone [and] building relationships with my customers,” she says.

Yeung and Spicer say they don’t take salaries from their new businesses yet. Instead, they’ve made lifestyle sacrifices, they say: Spicer’s girlfriend now shoulders the couple’s expenses, and Yeung moved into a cheaper apartment with a new roommate to cut costs.

Both currently prefer the uncertainty of entrepreneurship to their former roles, they say. Headlines about companies like Amazon, Salesforce and Block — which cited AI while cumulatively laying off tens of thousands of employees over the past year — partially fueled Spicer’s decision to leave his previous career, he says.

Corporate employment is less stable than it used to be, feeding some people’s inclinations to strike out on their own, says Todd McCracken, president and CEO of the National Small Business Association, an advocacy group. The U.S. added 116,000 jobs in 2025, down from 1.46 million in 2024. Job cuts announced in January reached their highest monthly level at the start of a year since 2009, according to data from global outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.
“In terms of national culture, I think there’s been this drift away from large, bureaucratic institutions into entrepreneurship and startup culture,” McCracken says.
While AI may threaten some workers’ job stability, it can also help aspiring entrepreneurs start businesses, says Chaudhuri.

The technology can help create basic websites or business plans, no prior expertise required, he says. In some contexts, it can handle basic, fundamental tasks — often administrative — that founders would otherwise need to spend extra time doing themselves, or hire and pay people to do.

Shahezad Contractor is the founder and CEO of Philadelphia-based halal restaurant group Cousin’s Food Inc., which brought in more than $4 million in combined 2025 revenue, according to documents reviewed by CNBC Make It. He regularly uses AI tools, particularly LLMs like Claude, to generate social media content ideas, create training materials for employees and write marketing copy, he says.

“Previously, maybe I would have hired a content writer” for some of those functions, says Contractor, 44, but AI helps him “fill in the gaps” in his skill set and do it himself. He even uses AI to scout new locations for his restaurant group — which currently includes a pizza and hoagie shop, a barbecue restaurant and eight burger joints — and to generate financial forecasts for his existing ones, he says.
Contractor previously worked in IT for 24 years. AI’s spread across the tech industry influenced his decision to leave his former career and pursue entrepreneurship in 2024, he says.

AI might help some small-business owners, but it won’t necessarily guarantee their success in the long run, says Benjamin Jones, an entrepreneurship and strategy professor at Northwestern University’s Kellogg School of Management. More startups lead to more competition — for preexisting companies, too, he notes.
Chaudhuri echoes the sentiment: “We’ve had more startups than ever in the past two decades, but the stock market is simultaneously more concentrated than ever.”
But entrepreneurship requires risk and failure, says Jones. “It’s just hard to know what’s going to work until you try,” he says. When you start a new business, “that’s the nature of the adventure.”

title: 188-year-old NYC pharmacy has been 'packed like sardines'—all because of $40 headbands and FX's 'Love Story'
author: Megan Sauer
description: Twenty-somethings are flocking to a nearly 200-year-old pharmacy in New York to buy headbands once worn by Carolyn Bessette Kennedy, the drugstore's owners say.
keywords: makeit, Articles, Comcast Corp, New York, First National Corp, John Jr., Walt Disney Co, Mattel Inc, Hasbro Inc, Ulta Beauty Inc, PVH Corp, Sally Beauty Holdings Inc, Estée Lauder Companies Inc, Coty Inc, CVS Health Corp, New Jersey, Make It, Make It - Success, Make It - Start-ups, source:tagname:CNBC US Source
paragraphs: On a normal weekday afternoon at C.O. Bigelow apothecary in New York’s Greenwich Village neighborhood, regulars and tourists traipse across the shop’s original tile flooring to pick up prescriptions, peruse luxury beauty products or chat with staff, some of whom have been there for over four decades.

The last month has been abnormal, say owners Ian and Alec Ginsberg, a father-and-son duo. Twenty-somethings are visiting the 188-year-old pharmacy in droves, gathering at the corner of the shop’s beauty counter where headbands are stocked. Most want one thing: A $40 1.5-inch tortoiseshell headband, the same style previously worn by Carolyn Bessette Kennedy, the former Calvin Klein publicist and wife of John F. Kennedy Jr, the store’s owners say.

On weekends since the Feb. 12 premiere of FX’s “Love Story: John F. Kennedy Jr. and Carolyn Bessette,” C.O. Bigelow has seen “traffic like the holidays,” says Ian Ginsberg, who has worked full-time at the store since 1985, when his own father owned it.

“Things [usually] ebb and flow in terms of foot traffic ... but this past weekend, the store was packed like sardines,” says Alec Ginsberg. “That’s not typical every single weekend of the year.” After “Love Story” premiered, sales rose at multiple other New York-based businesses associated with Bessette Kennedy, including eyeglass store Selima Optique and Panna II Garden Indian restaurant, Bloomberg reported on March 5.

Established brands or products tend to go viral when a new demographic sees them as offering something they haven’t discovered yet, says Jonah Berger, an associate marketing professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania.

These specific headbands may offer “a feeling of social currency” to some Gen Zers, showing the people around them that they’re culturally aware — up-to-date on a buzzy TV show and fluent in its cultural commentary — and can afford to show it, Berger says.
DON’T MISS: The leadership skills that can help you stand out at work

Some businesses are well-positioned to capitalize on cultural trends. Chinese toy brand Pop Mart sold roughly $423 million worth of Labubu dolls in 2024 after K-Pop star Lisa Manoban was spotted with one attached to her purse that April. In New York, tourists still visit 138-year-old Katz’s Deli to see the restaurant from the 1989 movie “When Harry Met Sally.”

And many Gen Zers have an affinity for in-person retail shopping. In 2025, consumers between 18 and 24 years old bought 62% of their total general merchandise purchases in stores, according to Circana data reported by the Wall Street Journal on March 9.
“We’re excited to see Gen Z discover retail,” says Ian Ginsberg.

The Ginsberg family has owned C.O. Bigelow since 1939, when Ian Ginsberg’s great-grandfather purchased the then-rundown pharmacy after the Great Depression, according to its website. In the 1970s, its proximity to recording studios attracted artists and performers to its lunch counter, and the shop became a sort of “cultural community gathering place,” Alec Ginsberg says.

In late 1980s, Ian Ginsberg decided that the store needed a differentiator, or it’d risk losing business to chain pharmacies that could sell “lighters, pens and Tylenol” at lower prices, he says. He chose a luxury twist, sourcing beauty products and hair accessories from Europe, including the headbands that Bessette Kennedy first purchased in the 1990s, he says.

Customers who walk into the store today should have a comparable experience as the customers who came in nearly 200 years ago, the owners say. In part, that means hiring personable and knowledgeable employees, including the Ginsbergs themselves: Ian Ginsberg once told his son that he’d need to attend pharmacy school to hold any significant role in the store, he says. The business has maintained several physical aspects of its store over the decades, including original gas-run chandeliers.

Prioritizing customer experience, especially in a way that’s authentic, can help brick-and-mortar stores survive retail upticks and downturns, says Joe Pine, an experience economy researcher, consultant and author. That customer experience can include buying a product, even as small as a hair accessory, that fulfills a shopper’s desire to look or feel a specific way, he says.
“People increasingly desire to buy things — physical goods, as well as services and experiences — that help them achieve their aspirations and become who they want to become,” says Pine.

C.O. Bigelow has sold out and restocked its tortoiseshell headband multiple times since the “Love Story” premiere, the owners say. Seconds after a customer plucks a black, brown or pearl headband out of a bowl or off a rack, a salesperson dutifully replaces it with a replica.

“It’s not like, all of a sudden, we saw the obsession with [Bessette Kennedy] and thought, ‘We should capitalize on this. Let’s do headbands again,’” says Alec Ginsberg. “The headbands have been exactly where they’ve been for 30 years.”

Twenty-somethings are visiting the 188-year-old pharmacy in droves, gathering at the corner of the shop’s beauty counter where headbands are stocked. Most want one thing: A $40 1.5-inch tortoiseshell headband, the same style previously worn by Carolyn Bessette Kennedy, the former Calvin Klein publicist and wife of John F. Kennedy Jr, the store’s owners say.
	On weekends since the Feb. 12 premiere of FX’s “Love Story: John F. Kennedy Jr. and Carolyn Bessette,” C.O. Bigelow has seen “traffic like the holidays,” says Ian Ginsberg, who has worked full-time at the store since 1985, when his own father owned it.
	“Things [usually] ebb and flow in terms of foot traffic ... but this past weekend, the store was packed like sardines,” says Alec Ginsberg. “That’s not typical every single weekend of the year.” After “Love Story” premiered, sales rose at multiple other New York-based businesses associated with Bessette Kennedy, including eyeglass store Selima Optique and Panna II Garden Indian restaurant, Bloomberg reported on March 5.
	Established brands or products tend to go viral when a new demographic sees them as offering something they haven’t discovered yet, says Jonah Berger, an associate marketing professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania.
	These specific headbands may offer “a feeling of social currency” to some Gen Zers, showing the people around them that they’re culturally aware — up-to-date on a buzzy TV show and fluent in its cultural commentary — and can afford to show it, Berger says.
	DON’T MISS: The leadership skills that can help you stand out at work
	Some businesses are well-positioned to capitalize on cultural trends. Chinese toy brand Pop Mart sold roughly $423 million worth of Labubu dolls in 2024 after K-Pop star Lisa Manoban was spotted with one attached to her purse that April. In New York, tourists still visit 138-year-old Katz’s Deli to see the restaurant from the 1989 movie “When Harry Met Sally.”
	And many Gen Zers have an affinity for in-person retail shopping. In 2025, consumers between 18 and 24 years old bought 62% of their total general merchandise purchases in stores, according to Circana data reported by the Wall Street Journal on March 9.
	“We’re excited to see Gen Z discover retail,” says Ian Ginsberg.
	The Ginsberg family has owned C.O. Bigelow since 1939, when Ian Ginsberg’s great-grandfather purchased the then-rundown pharmacy after the Great Depression, according to its website. In the 1970s, its proximity to recording studios attracted artists and performers to its lunch counter, and the shop became a sort of “cultural community gathering place,” Alec Ginsberg says.
	In late 1980s, Ian Ginsberg decided that the store needed a differentiator, or it’d risk losing business to chain pharmacies that could sell “lighters, pens and Tylenol” at lower prices, he says. He chose a luxury twist, sourcing beauty products and hair accessories from Europe, including the headbands that Bessette Kennedy first purchased in the 1990s, he says.
	Customers who walk into the store today should have a comparable experience as the customers who came in nearly 200 years ago, the owners say. In part, that means hiring personable and knowledgeable employees, including the Ginsbergs themselves: Ian Ginsberg once told his son that he’d need to attend pharmacy school to hold any significant role in the store, he says. The business has maintained several physical aspects of its store over the decades, including original gas-run chandeliers.
	Prioritizing customer experience, especially in a way that’s authentic, can help brick-and-mortar stores survive retail upticks and downturns, says Joe Pine, an experience economy researcher, consultant and author. That customer experience can include buying a product, even as small as a hair accessory, that fulfills a shopper’s desire to look or feel a specific way, he says.
	“People increasingly desire to buy things — physical goods, as well as services and experiences — that help them achieve their aspirations and become who they want to become,” says Pine.
	C.O. Bigelow has sold out and restocked its tortoiseshell headband multiple times since the “Love Story” premiere, the owners say. Seconds after a customer plucks a black, brown or pearl headband out of a bowl or off a rack, a salesperson dutifully replaces it with a replica.
	“It’s not like, all of a sudden, we saw the obsession with [Bessette Kennedy] and thought, ‘We should capitalize on this. Let’s do headbands again,’” says Alec Ginsberg. “The headbands have been exactly where they’ve been for 30 years.”
